Last updated November 14, 2026.

We buy Hennepin County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Who bills and collects property tax

Value and billing live in separate offices. Worth and classification are the assessor's call. Money goes to the treasurer at the Government Center. General questions go to the tax information line, 612-348-3011, which answers weekdays until 4:30, or to taxinfo@hennepin.us.

Your parcel is taxed by a stack of overlapping governments: the county, your city, your school district and often a few special districts. Over 70 local bodies set levies in Hennepin, and the auditor converts those levies and the assessment roll into one rate per district. Your statement adds them together. Two similar houses a few miles apart can therefore get quite different bills.

Hennepin County housing at a glance

No Minnesota county has more people than Hennepin: 1,284,784 as of July 2025, living in 587,984 housing units. Roughly 62.7% of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median owner-occupied value is $392,900. Twenty-two school districts overlap the county, among them Minneapolis, Edina, Minnetonka, Wayzata, Osseo Area and Anoka-Hennepin, and your district shows up as a line on the bill. Hopkins, Maple Grove and north Minneapolis each run on their own local rules, so begin with the city named on your statement.

Due dates and penalties

Expect two bills a year in Hennepin: spring money by May 15, fall money by October 15. A deadline that lands on a weekend or holiday rolls forward one business day. Minnesota Statutes 279.01 sets this pattern for any parcel owing over $100.

A late half gets hit the next day with 2 percent if the home is a homestead and 4 percent if it is anything else. On the first of the next month that charge repeats at the same size, and every month after that through December adds 1 percent more. Homestead penalties stop at 8 percent, nonhomestead at 12 percent. The county credits a late payment to penalty before it credits tax.

There is one way out. You can ask for a penalty abatement on a late half once every ten years, but only after the whole tax is paid and only if no older year is unpaid on the parcel.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hennepin County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay

Real property accounts can be paid on the county website by e-check, card, PayPal or Venmo, and the day you submit is the day it counts. Mobile home and personal property accounts need another route.

  • E-check has no fee, with a ceiling of $50,000 per transaction.
  • Cards, PayPal and Venmo top out at $25,000 per transaction. Visa debit picks up a $2.95 flat charge and the other electronic methods 2.29%, which the processor keeps.
  • At the counter: 300 South 6th Street, 6th floor of the Government Center, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Paying by card there costs 2.49%.
  • Checks made out to Hennepin County Treasurer can go in the drop box on that floor, available weekdays 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • Phone 1-877-626-0017, or mail to Hennepin County Treasurer, A-600 Government Center, Minneapolis, MN 55487-0060, with a postmark no later than the due date.

Direct payment pulls from your bank account on May 15 and October 15 each year. The enrollment form has to be in by April 15 for the spring half and September 15 for the fall half.

How to appeal your valuation

Market value is fixed as of January 2, and the notice reaches your mailbox in March. Each property gets a physical walk-through on a five-year cycle. Today's value sets next year's tax, which makes a high-looking notice worth a close read.

Your first move is a call to the assessor whose number is on the notice, or a visit to an open book session if your city offers one. If you still disagree, write to or appear before the local board of appeal and equalization, and after that the county board, which meets in mid-June. To get on the county board's list, call 612-348-7050 or email countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us before the date shown on the notice. Court is the other path: Minnesota Tax Court, or a district court petition that Minnesota Statutes 278.01 requires by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Yearly rhythm of a Hennepin tax bill
WhenWhat happens
January 2Value and classification fixed
MarchNotices and tax statements go out
April to MayAssessor calls, open book sessions, local boards
May 15First half due
Mid JuneCounty board of appeal and equalization
October 15Second half due
Mid to late NovemberNext year's proposed levies announced
November 25 and afterTruth-in-taxation hearings

Which cities run their own assessor?

Six cities handle assessment themselves, and an owner there calls the city instead of the county. Everywhere else the county assessor at 612-348-3046 answers the question.

  • Bloomington, 952-563-8722
  • Brooklyn Park, 763-493-8175
  • Eden Prairie, 952-949-8511
  • Minneapolis, 612-673-3000
  • Minnetonka, 952-939-8220
  • St. Louis Park, 952-924-2535

The notice mailed to the property names the right office, so look at it before you dial and save yourself a wasted call during the spring window.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Hennepin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

No deed gets recorded while back taxes are owed. Under Minnesota Statutes 272.12 the auditor reviews every deed headed for transfer, and the recorder will not take it without the auditor's note that nothing delinquent is outstanding. The recording checklist spells this out too.

This year's bill works differently. Splitting off a piece of a parcel calls for a treasurer's certification under Statutes 272.121 that the whole parcel's current tax is paid. For an ordinary sale of the whole lot, your title company decides how the year gets divided between you and the buyer. Request a county payoff figure if a half is still open. For an inherited house or one several years behind, ask for the payoff early so no surprise number stalls closing.

Homestead and ways to lower the bill

Homestead status saves the most. To qualify you need a Social Security or individual taxpayer identification number, ownership in your own name instead of a business entity, and either you or a relative living in the home. Qualifying homes get a lower classification rate, a reduced taxable market value and eligibility for the state property tax refund.

If you recently bought, look up your parcel on the county property map and send in a change form when the taxpayer name or mailing address is wrong. Property Watch is an email alert that pings you each time a document is recorded against your parcel, handy while you wait for an old loan release to be filed.

A seller's checklist

Run through this list before you put a sign in the yard. Pull the latest statement and copy down the parcel number. See whether both halves are paid, and if not, what is left. Find out if your city assesses its own property, because that decides who you phone. Ask the closing agent how this year's tax will be divided with the buyer. For an inherited or empty house, get a written payoff from the treasurer instead of trusting an old statement.

Bring the statement and your closing date to any call. The county can then quote a figure that matches what the title company will request, instead of one you have to redo a week later.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When do I pay Hennepin County property tax?

Spring and fall: May 15 and October 15. If either falls on a day off, you get the following business day. Mailed checks count when postmarked by the deadline.

Is a sale possible with Hennepin County taxes still owed?

Yes, but the overdue tax gets cleared first, since the auditor will not release a deed while delinquent tax shows on the parcel. Most sellers simply have the payoff deducted from proceeds at closing.

What is the first step to dispute a Hennepin County value?

Phone the assessor listed on the March notice. If that goes nowhere, the local board or the county board of appeal and equalization is next, and the county board wants a call to 612-348-7050 or an email to countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us before the notice date.

What does it cost to pay Hennepin County tax with a card?

Paying online with Visa debit costs a $2.95 flat fee, other electronic methods cost 2.29%, and the processor keeps it. An online e-check costs nothing. Cards at the 6th floor counter run 2.49%.

Where do I get answers about my Hennepin County tax bill?

Try 612-348-3011 or taxinfo@hennepin.us on weekdays. Valuation questions go to the assessor at 612-348-3046, unless your city does its own assessing.

Ramsey County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Ramsey County, MN Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Ramsey County, MN Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Ramsey County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Ramsey County?
We buy Ramsey County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Who handles property tax

Most of the county's tax work happens in the Plato Building at 90 Plato Blvd. West in Saint Paul, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Property Tax Services (651-266-2222) mails statements, takes payments and reviews penalty requests. The County Assessor (651-266-2131) estimates value and class. A separate line, 651-266-2002, covers delinquent tax information.

The same building also houses the Recorder, the Examiner of Titles and the tax-forfeited land office, so a seller who needs a payoff and then a recorded deed can finish most errands under one roof. Bring the parcel number, your ID and the closing date, and ask for the payoff and the current-year installment status together. The county's online Property Tax and Value Lookup lets you check taxes and values by parcel.

Ramsey County housing and the 2026 assessment

Saint Paul is the county seat and largest city, and Ramsey is the state's most densely settled county. Population is 541,623, down 1.9% from the 2020 base. There are 238,541 housing units across 221,327 households, and only 60.6% are owner-occupied. Median owner-occupied value is $326,600, median gross rent is $1,329, and median household income is $81,568.

With nearly four in ten households renting, buyers read the tax statement closely, and a seller should have it ready.

The 2026 Assessor's Report shows total assessed value of real property up by $1.4 billion to $78.12 billion, the highest figure in county history, even after a $66.9 million decline in apartment value. The 2026 values rest on sales that closed during 2025. If your notice showed a bigger jump than your neighbors', the Assessor can explain what drove the change on your parcel. Appraisers walk properties through the year to keep the data consistent, following state requirements for on-site inspections.

Notices and upcoming dates

Every owner gets two mailings per parcel. In mid-March comes the tax statement showing the first and second half for the year, together with the value notice that sets next year's tax. The second mailing, in November, is the proposed tax notice with the amounts being considered for the following year and the dates of budget meetings. Owners who sign up for eNoticesOnline receive them electronically.

Proposed notices for 2027 are delivered between November 11 and 24. The county's public hearing on its proposed 2027 supplemental budget and levy is Thursday, December 3 at 6 p.m. at the Saint Paul City Hall and Ramsey County Courthouse, 15 W Kellogg Blvd. Comments there are passed to the cities, school districts and other taxing bodies.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Ramsey County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How do I dispute my value?

Your first move is a call to the Assessor at 651-266-2131, since many questions end there. Here is what to expect:

  • You will not reach an appraiser right away.
  • Staff will ask what your concern is.
  • An appraiser should call you back within three days.

You can mail or email supporting papers such as a recent appraisal or a purchase record. The appraiser will say which format works best. If the phone review does not settle it, the county's appeals page describes open book meetings and formal petitions. Keep paying the tax while a petition is pending, or it can be dismissed automatically. Board dates print on each value notice, so confirm them with the Assessor.

Due dates and penalties

Homes are billed in two installments. The first half is due May 15 and the second half October 15, and a weekend due date moves to the next business day. If a bill totals $100 or less, all of it is due in the spring. Manufactured homes pay August 31 and November 15. Partial payments are taken, and late payments go to penalty first, then to tax. A returned payment costs $30.

Ramsey County penalties on homestead and cabin property
Payment date passesFirst half unpaidSecond half unpaid
May 162%none yet
July 15%none yet
October 18%none yet
October 168%2%
November 18%4%
December 18%5%
January 2, 202710%7%

Nonhomestead property starts at 4% after May 15 and tops out at 12% before year-end, rising to 14% in January.

Can the county waive a late penalty?

The county allows one waiver. An owner may request one penalty waiver per parcel every ten years, for either the first or the second half but not both. A first-half request must arrive between May 16 and October 15, and a second-half request between October 16 and December 20. You sign the form and send it with the payment, postmarked or dropped off by the deadline. The county refuses the waiver if the payment bounced, if the parcel has delinquent tax or a payment-plan contract, or if the waiver was used in the last ten years.

Separately, owners can ask the Auditor/Treasurer for an abatement of penalty, interest or costs in cases of exceptional hardship, such as a hospital stay. Call 651-266-2222 to ask. If the county says no, staff will walk through other relief and can set up a partial payment schedule.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ramsey County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with unpaid property tax

Tax turns delinquent on January 1 of the following year. The county then adds interest at 10 percent a year, plus a $25 delinquent fee for publication and notice. Owners have three years to redeem the property before the forfeiture process begins. Notice comes four ways: a courtesy letter in the first week of April, a published list of parcels in a county newspaper for two weeks in May, service of notice by the sheriff, and a certified letter in June.

A Confession of Judgment is the county's formal payment plan. The auditor decides whether it runs five or ten years, a $100 processing fee applies per contract, and interest is 7 percent a year on the unpaid balance. Current tax must be paid on time each year, and an owner can make no more than two such contracts on one parcel. Vacant land is not eligible.

Before listing, call Delinquent Tax Information at 651-266-2002 for the exact payoff. Minnesota Statutes 272.12 bars a recorder from taking most deeds until the auditor confirms no delinquent tax exists on the land. A cash sale moves faster, but it does not skip that check, and the payoff call is still the first thing to do. If the balance sits under a payment plan, ask the county how the remaining contract amount is handled at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Ramsey County property tax office?

Property Tax Services is in the Plato Building, 90 Plato Blvd. West, Saint Paul, MN 55107. It is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the phone is 651-266-2222.

Does Ramsey County take partial property tax payments?

Yes. Partial payments are accepted on an installment, with penalty paid off first and then tax. Making them does not stop penalties from growing on the unpaid part, so pay the balance by the due date if you can.

How many years does a Ramsey County owner have to redeem delinquent property?

Three years. Before 2014, homestead, cabin and township property had five years. Notice goes out in April, May and June before forfeiture.

When do Ramsey County's proposed 2027 tax notices arrive?

Between November 11 and 24, 2026. They show the estimated 2027 tax and the meetings where budgets are discussed. The county's own hearing is December 3 at 6 p.m.

Can I ask Ramsey County to forgive a late fee twice?

The standard waiver is once per parcel every ten years. A hardship abatement request is separate and can be made whether or not the waiver was used, but the county grants them mainly for exceptional hardship.

Dakota County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Dakota County, MN Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Dakota County, MN Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Dakota County, MN Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Dakota County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Dakota County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Dakota County?
We buy Dakota County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who to call

The work is split between two county groups. Assessing Services sets value and classification (651-438-4200). Property Taxation & Records bills, collects and handles delinquent years (651-438-4576). Both serve walk-in visitors at the Administration Center in Hastings, the county seat, at 1590 Highway 55.

Dakota County is the third most populous county in Minnesota, home to about 457,710 people, with Lakeville its largest city.

Dakota County housing and what it means for pricing

Dense suburbs fill the north of the county, and farmland and small towns fill the south. Burnsville, Eagan, Apple Valley, Lakeville, Rosemount and Hastings are among the larger cities. Farmington, Hampton, Randolph and Miesville keep an older street grid.

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home is $381,000.
  • Median household income is $106,318, and median gross rent is $1,548.
  • Owner-occupied housing makes up 74.9% of the stock, out of 185,931 housing units.

A higher home value usually means a larger tax bill, so read your statement before you set a price. The county's Tax Estimator page lets you test a number.

Due dates

Real property tax is due May 15 and October 15. Agricultural land and manufactured homes have a second-half date of November 15, which moves to Monday, November 16 this year because the 15th is a Sunday.

Dakota County property tax due dates by property type
Property typeFirst halfSecond half
Real propertyMay 15Oct. 15
Manufactured homeAug. 31Nov. 16
AgriculturalMay 15Nov. 16
Personal propertyMay 15none
Personal property on government-owned landMay 15Oct. 15

A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before the due date, or penalties apply. Under Minnesota Statutes section 279.01, homestead tax picks up 2% after the due date and non-homestead picks up 4%.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Dakota County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay

Five payment routes are available, each with its own cost.

  • Online or by phone through Paymentus (1-844-797-9075): cards carry a 2.29% convenience fee, Visa debit a $2.95 fee, and a bank transfer $0.35. Each transaction tops out at $100,000.
  • In person at the Administration Center in Hastings, the Northern Service Center in West St. Paul, or the Western Service Center in Apple Valley, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. Cards carry a 2.49% fee.
  • By mail to Property Taxation & Records, Attn: Taxation, 1590 Highway 55, Hastings, MN 55033-2343.
  • Automatic withdrawal, free, for owners whose lender does not pay the tax and who have no overdue tax. Forms filed now apply to taxes due in 2027, and a cancellation is due 15 days before a due date.

To see what you owe, enter just your house number in the Property Information Search.

When taxes go unpaid

Tax still open on January 2 becomes delinquent, and interest is added monthly. A judgment, which works as a tax lien, is entered against the property. Owners get a letter in March, and the list of delinquent parcels runs in a local newspaper for two weeks.

From there the owner has three years to pay in full or set up a payment plan. If a balance remains after that, the property forfeits to the State of Minnesota, and the county manages it for the state. Notices to owners with long-open years go out by sheriff's service, so do not ignore a letter.

Penalty abatement is possible but narrow. The county considers clerical error, hardship such as a death or serious illness, a government-declared emergency, a postal error admitted in writing, and a stop-payment on a lost check made within 30 days. It will not accept a missing statement, a late payment alone, or general financial hardship.

How to appeal your value

The informal review and the Special County Board of Appeal and Equalization both happen in the spring and early summer. Once that board adjourns, Assessing Services can no longer change that year's value, so a late request affects the next assessment, with taxes payable the year after.

The Minnesota Tax Court is the formal option that remains. Section 278.01 requires a copy to be served on the county auditor, with the petition and proof of service filed with the court administrator by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Dakota County accepts email service at taxpetitions@co.dakota.mn.us and advises filing early, because the county emails back an acknowledgment that must be filed with the court. Bring recent appraisals or sales of similar homes as evidence, and call the Tax Court at 651-539-3260 with questions.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Dakota County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Relief programs and their deadlines

The county's Home and Property page groups its relief programs and lists a date for most of them. Missing one usually means waiting a full year.

  • Homestead, for owners who live in the house, with applications due December 31.
  • Blind and disabled homestead (Class 1b), due October 1.
  • Green Acres, due May 1, and Agricultural Preserves, due June 1.
  • Senior citizen property tax deferment, the disabled-service exclusion, open spaces and property tax exemption, plus state property tax refunds and local option disaster abatement.

The open book appeal runs from March 11 to May 1, and manufactured home homestead applications are due May 29. The county also posts proposed taxes for 2027 on its Home and Property page.

The tax bill at closing

Cities and townships set their own sale rules, especially for wells, septic systems, manufactured homes and owners on Medical Assistance, whose certificate of clearance line is 651-554-6555. Under section 272.12, the county auditor must confirm there is no delinquent tax before a deed is recorded, and the county can send a deed back if tax is owed.

A buyer who plans to live in the house should mark the homestead date of December 31 on a calendar. Sellers can help by giving the buyer the Assessing Services number early in the process.

To get ready, look up the parcel in the Property Information Search, confirm both halves of the current year are paid, and ask Property Taxation & Records about older years. Bring that information to your title company so the payoff is simple to pull from proceeds. If the house is a manufactured home or sits on a well or septic system, ask your city or township about its sale rules at the same time.

Frequently asked questions

What is the next Dakota County property tax deadline?

Real property is due May 15 and October 15 each year. Agricultural property and manufactured homes are due November 15, moved to the next business day when that is a weekend. Homestead applications are due December 31.

Can I still appeal my Dakota County value?

After the county board meets in June, only the Minnesota Tax Court is left. A petition on taxes payable in 2027 is due by April 30, 2027, and Assessing Services can change only the later assessment.

How do I pay Dakota County property tax by phone?

Call 1-844-797-9075 and use a Discover, MasterCard or Visa card at 2.29%, a Visa debit at $2.95, or a bank transfer at $0.35. Your payment is complete only once you receive a confirmation number.

How long before Dakota County can take a property for unpaid tax?

Owners have three years from the delinquency to pay or set up a payment plan before the property forfeits to the state. Interest builds monthly during that time. Call 651-438-4576 about your parcel.

Does Dakota County give a free way to check my balance?

Yes. The Property Information Search is free, and you enter only your house number to see what you owe. Property Taxation & Records can help at taxation@co.dakota.mn.us or 651-438-4576. A free paperless notice option sends your statement by email.

Where to pay a Washington County property tax bill

Property Records and Taxpayer Services runs the tax counter at the Government Center, 14949 62nd Street North in Stillwater, with a phone line at 651-430-6175.   • Central Service Center, 1261 Woodlane Drive, Woodbury
  • Cottage Grove Service Center, 13000 Ravine Parkway
  • Headwaters Service Center, 19955 Forest Road North, Forest Lake

Boxes are emptied the next business day, so a payment dropped after hours on the last day should not be counted on. The same office also takes homestead applications at each of those locations. If you would rather not travel at all, online payment is available any hour, and the confirmation serves as your record.

Housing in Washington County

Washington County is the eastern edge of the metro, bounded by the St. Croix River and Wisconsin, with Stillwater as the seat and Woodbury the largest of its 25 cities. Population was 286,895 in July 2025, up 7.2% since the 2020 base. There are 115,270 housing units, and owners live in 81.3% of them. The median owner-occupied value is $422,000, and owners with a mortgage pay $2,275 a month at the median. Median gross rent is $1,710, and builders took out 2,382 permits in 2025.

At those values a one percent shift in assessed value moves the tax bill by a meaningful sum, so read the March valuation notice carefully before any listing decision.

Due dates and penalties

Most real estate is split into two equal payments. Agricultural land has its second half on November 15, manufactured homes pay on August 31 and November 15, and personal property is due in full May 15 for most owners. An ordinary house pays its second half in October, so confirm that payment posted before you list. A proposed-tax notice, the Truth in Taxation notice, is mailed in mid-November.

Washington County penalty ladder for homestead and cabin property
If paid on or afterFirst halfSecond half
May 162%none yet
June 14%none yet

Non-homestead rates run higher, reaching 12% on the first half by October 1. Once January 2 passes, interest starts on unpaid tax, penalties and fees at an annual 8%, rising monthly.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Washington County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How a Washington County appeal works

Each spring the valuation notice rides in the same envelope as the tax statement, mailed by March 31. Call the appraisers at 651-430-6175 first, since many questions end there. An in-person review of the property is required before any adjustment. After that the path depends on where the home sits.

  1. Cities and townships with a local board, such as Hugo, Forest Lake and Lake Elmo, hold hearings in April and expect you to appear if you want to keep the right to go further.
  2. Other places, including Woodbury, Stillwater, Oakdale and Cottage Grove, use regional open book sessions in April, where attendance is optional.
  3. The County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets in June at 5 p.m. at the Government Center. An appointment is needed by May 1.
  4. The Minnesota Tax Court takes petitions through April 30 of the year taxes are payable.

A petition has to be served on the county auditor under section 278.01. Washington County prefers its online upload portal, which returns an acknowledgment of service within roughly 5 to 10 minutes. Email and fax are not accepted, and a petition left in the drop box is not service. Owners of income-producing property also owe disclosure documents by August 1.

What happens if taxes go unpaid?

Tax unpaid after December 31 becomes delinquent on January 2, and the county starts proceedings in the spring with a letter and a published list of delinquent parcels. A $25 fee covers that notice. The first year of delinquency starts a three-year redemption period, and a property that is not redeemed forfeits to the State of Minnesota. The final notice adds a $150 fee, and the sheriff delivers a copy to anyone living there.

A Confession of Judgment lets an owner, a lender, a contract for deed buyer or a life estate holder repay over time. The auditor assigns a ten-year plan for residential parcels with 10% down, or a five-year plan for commercial parcels with 20% down. The current year's tax and the yearly installment must both be paid by December 31 to stay in good standing.

Relief programs that affect a sale

The homestead market value exclusion was increased beginning with taxes payable in 2025, and it shrinks as value rises. Non-homestead property carries higher penalty rates in the county table, so classification matters when a sale closes close to a deadline.

Two state refunds are for owners who live in their property. The standard Property Tax Refund had an income limit of $142,490 for 2025. The special refund requires a net tax increase of at least 12% and $100, and increases caused by improvements do not count. Forms and instructions are on the Minnesota Department of Revenue website. A buyer who will live in the home may ask about these refunds, so it helps to know which ones depend on income and which on a jump in the tax bill.

Settling tax at a Washington County closing

Buyers are told to verify that tax due in the year of sale has been paid, covering the usual May 15 and October 15 halves. Under section 272.12 the auditor certifies delinquent tax before a deed is recorded. Ask the taxpayer services line for a payoff figure during the listing period, and have the title company show the year's split on the closing statement.

If you are selling to a cash buyer, the same certification applies, so request the payoff early. A balance found at the last minute is the most common reason a closing date slips.

Frequently asked questions

Can I pay my Washington County taxes in Woodbury instead of Stillwater?

Yes. The Woodbury service center on Woodlane Drive takes tax payments, as do the Cottage Grove and Forest Lake centers. A box payment is collected the next business day, so mail or pay online if the deadline is today.

What interest does Washington County charge on delinquent tax?

Interest runs at an annual rate of 8% on unpaid tax, penalties and fees beginning January 2, increasing monthly. Penalty percentages also step up on that date, so a balance grows quickly.

How do I serve a tax petition on Washington County?

Use the county's online petition portal, which returns an acknowledgment in a few minutes, or hand it to staff at the Government Center counter during business hours. Email and fax are not accepted, and the April 30 deadline is strict.

Is there a payment plan for back taxes in Washington County?

Yes, a Confession of Judgment. A residential parcel gets ten years with 10% down, and a commercial parcel gets five years with 20% down. The owner, a lender, a contract for deed buyer or a life estate holder may apply.

When does the Washington County Board of Appeal meet?

In June at 5 p.m. at the Government Center in Stillwater. An appointment is needed by May 1 by calling 651-430-6175, and the dates appear on the valuation notice mailed in March.

Which office sends the bill

Property Records & Taxation handles everything under one roof, from valuation to collection. The office is in the Government Center at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303. Phone 763-323-5400 for tax questions, or write to proptax@anokacountymn.gov about a valuation. Counter service runs weekdays from eight in the morning until half past four, holidays excepted.

The county prints the proposed tax statements for many taxing bodies at once: the county itself, your city, the school district and the state, depending on where the parcel sits and what type of property it is. The bill you pay combines all of those levies. See the Taxation page for details.

Local context for sellers

Anoka County sits north of Hennepin and Ramsey counties and holds twenty cities and one township. Population is 381,605. There are 145,902 housing units, with 80.2% occupied by owners. Owned homes have a median value of $346,500, rent is $1,464 at the median, and household income is $101,869. The valuation appeal route depends on which city a house is in.

How the county values and classifies a home

The assessor values property as of January 2 each year and mails a Notice of Valuation and Classification. The estimated market value on that notice is what the assessor thinks the property would sell for on the open market. The class records how the property is used.

On a homestead, the notice also shows a Homestead Market Value Exclusion. The formula gives a maximum of $38,000 at a market value of $95,000, falling by nine percent of the value above $95,000, and disappearing at $517,200. A house worth more than that gets no exclusion, so a buyer in that range will see the full taxable value.

The notice lists other adjustments too, including a disability exclusion, deferrals under Green Acres, Rural Preserve and Open Space, and a platted vacant land deferral. Taxable market value is the figure after all of those. A separate line shows new improvement value, the assessor's estimate of additions made in the past five years.

A higher value does not automatically raise your bill. Taxes follow the annual levy and how your value moves compared with neighboring properties.

How to appeal your valuation

The path depends on your city, and your valuation notice tells you which option applies.

  • In a city that holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there first if you want to go on to the county board.
  • In an Open Book city, you can skip straight to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June.
  • Either way, the County Board of Appeal and Equalization is the next stop if the first step did not settle things.

For a first conversation about the number itself, write to proptax@anokacountymn.gov or call 763-323-5400. Have your parcel identification number ready.

Beyond the boards, Minnesota Statutes 278.01 lets an owner petition district court or the Tax Court by serving the county auditor, with proof of service filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Statute 274.01 keeps local board meetings between April 1 and May 31.

Payment methods

You can pay four ways: at PayAnokaCounty online, by mail, at the Government Center, or through a free automatic direct payment program.

Mail is sometimes not postmarked on the day it is dropped off. If the deadline is close, ask the post office counter for a hand-applied postmark, which is free. There is no grace period, and a due date that falls on a weekend moves to the first business day after the weekend. Due dates depend on how the property is classified.

Proposed statements and levy hearings

Proposed statements are mailed in mid-November. They are not final until the taxing bodies approve their levies in December. Budget and levy hearing dates are posted on the county Taxation page, and eNotices let an owner get the statement by email with the code printed on the proposed notice.

Four things move a bill: local levies from the city, school district and county, changes in the overall tax base, changes in your assessed value, and how your value change compares with others nearby. Hearings are for budgets, not valuations, so the Truth in Taxation meeting is not the place to argue your taxable market value.

A one-time increase of nearly 15% was created for homeowners who qualified for the 2025 regular property tax refund. Form M1PR is due by August 15, 2027.

Taxes after you sell

Often the statement still goes to you. The county mails one statement per parcel a year, in mid-March, and a change in recorded ownership after January 1 does not trigger a new mailing. The statement goes to the previous owner or taxpayer, so buyer and seller should plan for a duplicate request after closing.

A sale, a refinance or a mortgage satisfaction are the usual reasons for a different taxpayer, and each calls for a duplicate. Call 763-323-5400 if you have not received a statement by April 1. Not receiving one does not forgive the penalty or interest.

Sellers can keep this simple. Before listing, pull your latest notice and note the estimated market value, the class and any exclusion. Write down the parcel identification number, since the office will ask for it on every call. At closing, the title company usually prorates the current year between buyer and seller, and any gap shows up on the settlement statement. Keep a copy of your last statement for your records, and give the buyer the office phone number so the new owner can request a duplicate once the deed is recorded.

A manufactured home is taxed on a separate schedule, with statements mailed in July, and its title cannot be transferred until all current and delinquent personal property taxes are paid.

At closing, ask the title company to settle any unpaid balance from your proceeds. A cash sale moves faster, but the same balance still has to be cleared before the deed is recorded.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Anoka County property tax in person?

Go to the Government Center in Anoka at 2100 3rd Avenue on a weekday. A service counter and a payment drop box are available. Cash and checks carry no fee, while cards and mobile wallets add 2.6%.

Does Anoka County give a grace period on late taxes?

No. There is none, and a payment made after either due date draws a penalty that grows the later you pay.

What is the Anoka County assessment date?

January 2 each year. The value notice reflects what the assessor thinks the property would sell for at that time, and the back of the notice lists your appeal options.

Can I appeal at the Anoka County board without going to the city first?

Only if your city uses the Open Book format. Where a city holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there before the June county board hearing.

Is the Anoka County proposed tax statement my final bill?

No. The proposed statement shows what you would pay in 2027 if the taxing bodies approve the budgets they are considering. Levies are approved in December, and the final bill is mailed in mid-March.

Which Wright County office answers which tax question?

Finance and Taxpayer Services collects the money, and it works from the Government Center at 3650 Braddock Avenue NE, Suite 1400, in Buffalo (main line 763-682-7578). The Assessor, in Suite 1700 of the same building, handles every question about value and class. A drop box stands next to the License Center drive-through on the north side of the building. You can also pay online from the county's taxpayer FAQ. Copies of statements can be printed after you enter the property ID, or by calling 763-682-7577.

Wright County housing market

Wright County lies northwest of Minneapolis along the Mississippi River, with rolling land and many small lakes. Buffalo is the county seat. Otsego, with 19,966 people in 2020, is the largest city, followed by St. Michael, Buffalo and Monticello.

The county had 157,559 residents in July 2025, up 11.5% from 141,337 in 2020. Of 61,161 housing units, 84.1% are owner-occupied. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $358,900, and owners with a mortgage carry median monthly costs of $2,098. Builders pulled 1,156 permits in 2025. The county added 38.6% to its population in the 2000s and 13.3% in the 2010s, so values move fast. Compare your valuation notice with recent nearby sales before you list.

Due dates for Wright County property taxes

Real estate is paid on May 15 and October 15. Agricultural property is due May 15 and November 15, manufactured homes August 31 and November 15, and personal property May 15 and October 15, though some personal property is due in full in May. When the tax on a parcel is under $100, or under $50 for a manufactured home, the whole amount is due with the first half. A November date that falls on a weekend moves, so check the stub for the exact day.

Under state law the postmark is what counts. Many post offices now route mail through a servicing center, so a letter may not be stamped until two or three days after you drop it off. A payment mailed on the last day can therefore be late. Mail a week early, or pay online, and the risk goes away.

Statements for real estate are mailed by March 31. Manufactured home statements go out by July 15.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Wright County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Penalties on late payments

The county applies the penalty on the next business day after the due date, and the amount grows on the first of every month the tax stays unpaid. The chart on the back of your statement shows the figures, and the rates come from state law rather than local choice. Under section 279.01, homestead property starts at 2% and non-homestead at 4%, with the running total capped at 8% and 12%.

Tax left open through the end of the year brings further fees and interest, and the parcel lands on the delinquent tax list. Sellers should clear that first, because delinquent tax has to be paid before the auditor will certify a transfer.

How to appeal your Wright County valuation

Wright County mails valuation notices each spring. The assessor's appeals page advises gathering an appraisal, a market analysis or sales data from the right time frame. Then call the Assessor to confirm structure dimensions and condition, and ask how the value and class were set. If you still disagree, these are the stages:

  1. Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, held by some cities and townships in April or early May. Appearing in person or in writing preserves your right to go to the county.
  2. Open book meetings in jurisdictions that chose them, where you meet an appraiser and may skip straight to the county board.
  3. County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June. In 2026 it met on Monday, June 15, at 4 p.m. in the Government Center, with appointments required by June 8 so appraisers could inspect first.
  4. Minnesota Tax Court, which you may use directly or after the county board.

The notice itself explains the Homestead Market Value Exclusion, deferrals for programs such as Green Acres and an exclusion for military service disability. A petition to Tax Court must also meet the April 30 date in section 278.01.

Ditch and special assessments in a sale

Wright County keeps a system of official drainage ditches, and owners who benefit pay assessments on top of ordinary tax. The Finance Director links those property owners with the County Board, and questions about the charges go to 763-682-7583. Buyers should ask whether the parcel sits on a ditch system and how many annual installments remain.

Special assessments for streets, sewer or similar projects are handled at 763-682-7573. Both kinds appear on the tax statement, so ask the title company to request payoff figures before closing. Under section 272.12 the auditor must certify no delinquent tax before a deed can be recorded.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wright County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who owes the tax when a house changes hands?

Statements are addressed to the owner of record as of January 2, which may be the seller well into the year. Your settlement statement, or the title company that handled the closing, shows who is responsible for what. A buyer with a mortgage should confirm with the lender what has been paid from escrow, because a stub reading that taxes were sent to an escrow agent means no payment is due from you.

Property tax refunds belong to the State of Minnesota, and the county can't report on their status. The state number is 800-652-9094.

Before you list, pull a copy of your latest statement and note the property ID, the mailing address on file and whether escrow pays it. Give the title company those details at the start so payoff and proration figures are ready well before closing day. If the mailing address is stale, call 763-684-8617 and fix it, since the statement follows the owner of record.

A cash sale skips the lender, so there's no escrow to sort out. You still need the title company to prorate the current year and confirm nothing delinquent is on the parcel.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Wright County property tax payment deadline?

May 15 and October 15 for ordinary real estate, with agricultural land due in November. Call 763-682-7584 or 763-682-7572 for a balance and see your stub for the November date.

Does Wright County go by the postmark?

Yes. A payment postmarked by the due date is timely. Because post offices may not stamp mail for two or three days, the county urges people to mail early or pay online.

Who do I call about a Wright County special or ditch assessment?

Special assessments go to 763-682-7573 and ditch assessments to 763-682-7583. Both appear on the tax statement. The Finance Director is the contact point between ditch owners and the County Board.

When does the Wright County Board of Appeal meet?

In June. In 2026 it met Monday, June 15 at 4 p.m. at 3650 Braddock Avenue NE in Buffalo. Owners had to book by June 8 through the Assessor at 763-682-7367, and a local board or open book meeting comes first.

Why did I not get a Wright County tax statement after buying?

Statements go to the owner of record as of January 2. Look up the parcel online with its property ID or call 763-682-7577, and ask the title company or lender about escrow payments.

Who handles property tax in Scott County

Scott County's Property and Taxation Services department runs the whole process, from the assessors who set values to the staff who take payments. It sits in the Government Center in Shakopee, the county seat. Reach it at 952-496-8115 or propertytax@co.scott.mn.us.

Eleven assessors estimate market value and classification for roughly 58,000 parcels, and they also hold the public meetings where owners can discuss a value. Cities and townships such as Prior Lake, Savage, Jordan and Belle Plaine each add their own levy to the single statement a parcel receives, and so do the school districts and special districts that overlap them.

The county's assessment page has a short explainer on the move from the homestead market value credit to the homestead market value exclusion. Read it before you compare two years of statements.

Scott County housing snapshot

Scott County had an estimated 159,017 residents in July 2025, up from 150,928 in the 2020 census. It is a county of owners: 83.8 percent of the 54,971 households own their home. The typical owner-occupied home was worth $419,400 for 2020 to 2024, monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $2,329, and gross rent is $1,568. Builders pulled 883 permits in 2025 on top of 59,179 housing units, so newer subdivisions compete directly with resale houses.

Due dates and penalties

Scott County bills in two halves, mid-May and mid-October. After the October date the next deadline is the first half of the following year.

A half that goes unpaid is charged under Minnesota Statutes 279.01: 2 percent for a homestead and 4 percent for any other class, applied again at the start of the next month, with 1 percent monthly additions after that. Homesteads stop at 8 percent total and other property at 12 percent. One more rule helps late mailers: a county treasurer must forgive the penalty a single time if the postmark is within one business day of the deadline.

That waiver matters more now that the Postal Service dates mail when it first processes it. Scott County recommends that mailers carry the payment to a post office counter and ask for a manual postmark, mail several business days early, or pay electronically.

The best way to pay a Scott County bill

Paying online is quickest, and it saves a trip to Shakopee on a busy deadline. The online payment center takes e-check, debit and credit cards, and it will not work in the Internet Explorer browser.

  • If you wait for a receipt at the Government Center on the due date, staff add your name to a standby list, so use another route.
  • Mailed payments count as on time only with a postmark dated by the deadline.
  • If your parcel is under a confession of judgment contract, confirm any back-year amounts with taxation staff at 952-496-8115 first.
  • You can subscribe to e-notices through the same online payment center and get statements by email.

Whichever route you choose, keep the confirmation for your records.

How do I appeal my Scott County valuation?

Begin by gathering evidence that the value is too high, for example an appraisal or the sale price of a similar house nearby. Then call or visit the assessor who covers your city or township.

Next comes the Open Book session or the Local Board of Appeal and Equalization named on your value notice, and either one can lead on to the county board. After that, the Minnesota Tax Court takes petitions filed once the notice is in hand and no later than April 30 of the year the tax comes due.

The county takes service of a petition by email or in a drop box outside the Government Center, but anything that arrives after 4:30 p.m. on deadline day is ignored. Petitioners still have to file with the district court administrator, and the emailed acknowledgement doubles as proof of service. If no reply comes within 24 hours, follow up.

Selling a Scott County house with taxes owed

Back taxes remain on the parcel, so a seller who owes earlier years should get the figure from taxation staff before closing. The deed brings state costs of its own: under section 287.21 the deed tax is 0.33 percent of the price for most sales, with a flat $1.65 at $3,000 or below.

Recording also triggers a certificate of value for the county auditor (section 272.115). A buyer cannot get homestead status without it, and a sold house loses its homestead label for the next assessment year until the new owner applies and qualifies. Ask the closing agent how a half already paid is treated in the settlement figures.

Owners with tax owing, an inherited property or a house that needs repairs sometimes ask for a cash offer, and a buyer can work from the payoff figure the county gives you. Keep the statement and parcel number handy for that call.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Scott County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Paperwork to gather before you sell

Collect your latest statement, the parcel number and any value notice before you list. Call 952-496-8115 to ask for the payoff on any unpaid half and for the status of any confession of judgment contract. If you plan to dispute your value, know that the Open Book session and the local board come first, so bring your comparable sales to those meetings rather than waiting for the Tax Court deadline of April 30.

A cash sale skips the lender appraisal and much of the financing timeline, but the deed still needs a certificate of value, the deed tax, and a clean tax record before the Recorder will take it.

A simple order of work helps. Get the payoff figure first. Next, settle any open half so the balance is clear. Then give the closing agent the parcel number so the certificate of value can be filled in correctly. Last, once the deed is recorded, expect the new owner to apply for homestead, since your own label drops off for the next assessment year. If your tax statement still shows a homestead exclusion, mention that to the buyer so there are no surprises on their first bill. Keep copies of every payment confirmation until the sale has closed and the county shows the parcel as current.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Scott County property tax phone number?

Call the department at 952-496-8115, or write to propertytax@co.scott.mn.us.

When is the second half of Scott County property tax due?

Mid-October each year. After that date an unpaid balance is already drawing penalty.

What does online payment cost in Scott County?

E-check payments carry $1.50 per transaction and card payments carry 2.3 percent of the amount.

Where is the Scott County drop box for property tax?

The outdoor box is in the circular driveway off Atwood Street between 4th and 5th Avenue in Shakopee, next to the USPS mailbox. County libraries also hold a drop box in the weeks before each deadline.

What is the last step if I still disagree with my value?

A petition to the Minnesota Tax Court, due April 30 of the tax year. Serve a copy on Scott County and file it with the district court administrator.

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who handles property tax for a house in Stearns County?

Two county offices share the work. The Auditor-Treasurer sends the statements and takes the money, and the Property Assessment Services group sets each parcel's value and class. Call the Auditor-Treasurer's office for its current address, phone number and payment mailing address.

The county's property services page groups the tax tools in one place: the property taxes pages, a Land Management Division that handles property transfers and new tax parcels, a Property Management Portal for business partners, an aggregate tax page and the tax-forfeited property listings. The Land Management Division is the office that posts the ownership change on the tax roll after the deed is filed.

The tax pages cover address changes for statements, electronic statements, payment options, due dates, penalties, relief options and the senior deferral. Call the Auditor-Treasurer before you list so you know the balance on each half and whether a special assessment is attached to the parcel.

Housing in Stearns County

About 164,000 people live in the large central Minnesota county built around St. Cloud, up 3.7% since April 2020. Of its 68,027 housing units, owners occupy 67.9%, roughly two of every three homes. The median owner-occupied value is $273,400 and median gross rent is $1,068. Farms, lake lots and St. Cloud rentals pull that midpoint in different directions, so it says little about any one street. Builders took out 648 permits in 2025.

Due dates and late penalties

Real estate tax is split into a spring half and a fall half, and agricultural land gets until November 15 for the second half. Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01 a late half picks up a penalty that keeps growing each month.

Stearns County real estate payment dates and starting penalties
PaymentDue dateStarting penalty, homesteadStarting penalty, nonhomestead
First halfMay 152%4%
Second halfOctober 152%4%
Agricultural second halfNovember 152%4%

The penalty climbs month by month, up to 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead property. When November 15 lands on a weekend, ask the Auditor-Treasurer which day the county treats as the effective date before you mail a farmland check. A one-time break exists: mail postmarked within a business day of the deadline gets its penalty abated by the treasurer, if the owner has never used that abatement.

The county lists five ways to pay: online, payment plans, in person, through an escrow account and by U.S. mail. The counter is open on weekdays from eight in the morning until half past four. Tax-forfeited land is property that goes to the State of Minnesota after three years of nonpayment from the judgment year.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Stearns County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal a Stearns County valuation

The usual order is the assessment office in spring, the local board, and finally the county board. The county's tax programs menu lists a Local Board of Appeals and Open Book page, and Minnesota Statutes 274.01 sets the local meeting window between April 1 and May 31.

  • Review the valuation notice and compare your estimated market value with recent sales of similar homes nearby.
  • Ask the assessor for an informal second look at the value or class.
  • Appear at your local board of review, or at the open book session if your city or township transferred that duty to the county. Skipping the local step usually closes the county step.
  • If that fails, the county board of appeal and equalization hears the case, and section 274.13 lets it raise or lower a value and change a classification.

Neither board has power to grant an exemption or remove a parcel from the roll. Check classification as well as value. The county's assessment pages also describe the homestead application, the disability market value exclusion and the Green Acres and Rural Preserve programs.

Relief programs and extra taxes on a bill

Several items show up on or near a Stearns County bill. Use this list to ask the right office the right question.

  • Green Acres, Rural Preserve, Class 2c Managed Forest Land and the Sustainable Forest Incentive Act lower the taxable value on qualifying rural land.
  • A residential homestead calculator estimates tax on a single-family home from the municipality, school district and estimated market value.
  • A senior citizen deferral is posted as its own page for owners who struggle with the payment.
  • The county transportation sales tax and wheelage tax fund road projects, and they are county taxes, not part of the property tax line.
  • An aggregate removal tax applies to operators who haul gravel or similar material.

Find out which of these touch your parcel before you pick a list price. A program that ends at sale can change the buyer's first full-year bill.

Steps to take before listing

  1. Pull your latest valuation notice and compare the estimated market value with recent nearby sales.
  2. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer for the balance on each half, any special assessment and any delinquent amount.
  3. Confirm with the assessment office that the parcel is classed the way you use it, and ask which relief programs end at sale.
  4. If the house is rural, ask whether Green Acres or Rural Preserve applies, since a buyer who does not qualify could face a bigger bill.
  5. Decide where statements should go after closing and file the address change.

Having these answers ready makes your price easier to defend, since a clean tax record and a clear class leave a buyer little to negotiate over.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Stearns County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who owes the tax when a Stearns County house changes hands?

The seller owes the tax through the day of closing, and the buyer takes it from there. In Minnesota the first half covers the first part of the year, and the closing agent usually prorates the current year between the parties. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer for the amount due, any special assessment balance and whether any delinquent amount is on the parcel.

File an address change if statements should go somewhere new after the sale. Tax liens are recorded in county land records, and the county has a separate page on tax lien recording for state, federal and county liens. If a mortgage escrow pays the bill, the lender still gets a copy and the new owner needs to tell the county where to send the next one.

With a cash sale there is no lender to coordinate, so the title company handles the payoff directly. Give it the parcel number and the balance you got from the Auditor-Treasurer, and the proration can be settled the same day as the deed.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I get the phone number for the Stearns County Auditor-Treasurer?

It is listed on the county's property services page. Call that office for the current address and payment details.

Where do I mail a Stearns County property tax payment?

Address the check to the Stearns County Auditor-Treasurer, using the payment address printed on your tax statement. Mail it early so the postmark lands by the due date.

Does Stearns County have a homestead tax estimator?

Yes. The assessment pages include a residential homestead tax estimator that uses the tax rates for the city and school district you choose along with your estimated market value.

How long before unpaid Stearns County taxes lead to forfeiture?

Tax-forfeited land is property that passes to the State of Minnesota after three years of nonpayment from the judgment year. Call the Auditor-Treasurer at once if a balance is delinquent, because the timeline can differ by property class.

Where does a Stearns County owner find the open book appeal information?

On the county's Local Board of Appeals and Open Book page under the property assessment services menu. It sits beside the homestead and exemption pages.

Offices and contacts

Work is split between two county offices in the same Chaska building, 600 East 4th Street. Bills and payments belong to Property Tax at (952) 361-1910 or custsvc@carvercountymn.gov. For value, class or homestead, contact Property Assessment & Homesteading at (952) 361-1960 or assessment@carvercountymn.gov. Doors are open weekdays, 8:00am to 4:30pm, except government holidays.

The county mails statements by March 31 every year. If yours goes missing you still owe the penalty, which the county's penalty page stresses in bold type.

Due dates

Typical parcels pay in halves on May 15 and October 15. Farm property usually pays the second half November 15, while manufactured homes pay August 31 and November 15. Minn. Stat. 279.01 words the same dates as payment before May 16 and before October 16.

  • A statement postmarked April 25 or later pushes the first-half deadline out to 21 days after the postmark.
  • Tax of $100 or less is paid in one sum by the first-half date.
  • Seasonal recreational property in class 4c, if not used commercially, follows the homestead penalty schedule.
  • Farm second-half tax carries no penalty when paid by November 15.

There is only one statement. The second-half stub is on it, and the county does not mail another in the fall.

Late penalties

A late payment draws penalty from the following day, and the rate steps up on the first of each month. The county's schedule tops out at 14%. Here is how it runs for a first-half payment on a residential parcel.

First-half penalty by payment date, Carver County residential property
Paid on or afterHomesteadNon-homestead
May 162%4%
June 14%8%
July 15%9%
August 16%10%
September 17%11%
October 18%12%
January 210%14%

The county applies money to the first half, penalty included, before any of it reaches the second half.

  • A U.S. Postal Service postmark dated on or before the due date is the only proof accepted. Meter marks from private machines do not qualify.
  • Checks sent through a bank's bill-pay service often have no postmark, so they have to land at the county by the due date.
  • The online system rejects savings accounts, and one wrong digit in the parcel number can push a payment into penalty.

There is also a one-time forgiveness rule. A mailed payment postmarked within one business day after the due date, from an owner who has not used the rule before, must have its penalty abated by the treasurer (279.01, subd. 2).

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Carver County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to contest your valuation

Call the assessor first. From there the county lists four steps: the assessment office, then an open book session or local board, then the county board, and last a petition to Minnesota Tax Court. Tax Court is open to you directly at any point.

  1. January 2 is the valuation date for every parcel. The 2026 valuation, used for taxes payable in 2027, rests on sales from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025.
  2. March: the Notice of Valuation and Classification shows up with the tax statement.
  3. April and May: local boards sit. Their meetings fall between April 1 and May 31 and each must wrap up within 20 days (Minn. Stat. 274.01). Combined, a board can lower the assessor's total by no more than one percent.
  4. June: the county board meets. You qualify to appear only if you went to the local board, and the appointment must be booked before June 1.
  5. April 30: Tax Court filing deadline each year.

Each November, cities, townships, school districts and the county hold Truth in Taxation meetings, and their notices compare this year's tax with an estimate for next year.

Paying your bill

You can pay by mailed check, bank bill pay or the county's online system. A check dropped in the mail on the due date needs that day's U.S. postmark. Bill-pay money counts only if it arrives by the due date. Type the parcel number slowly, because a keying slip can carry a payment past the deadline, and remember the portal turns away savings accounts.

If you are listing soon, a quick plan helps. Pull your latest statement and note both stub dates. Check the class and homestead line on the March value notice, and mark your local board date. Confirm with Property Tax that nothing is owed from earlier years, since a prior-year balance surfaces at closing and can delay it. Having those papers ready lets a buyer's lender or a cash buyer's title company move without waiting on you.

Call (952) 361-1910 with questions about what is owed or how penalty is calculated.

Selling and homestead

Look at the closing papers to see who covers the year's tax, and make sure the full year is paid. The county's public access page shows statement copies and offers email reminders. For a payoff figure on anything past due, call (952) 361-1910.

Homestead does not stay with the house. Send the assessor a fresh application after a new owner, a trust move, a name change, or any owner added or removed. Statute 272.115 has the assessor strip homestead from a sold parcel for the coming assessment year unless the buyer applies and is approved. No certificate of value on file means no homestead for the buyer. A qualifying owner may get the homestead market value exclusion, which lowers taxable value.

Owing back taxes does not block a sale. Ask the closing agent to request the amount due from the property tax office before the closing date, since penalty rises monthly. A cash buyer can close quickly, but the same payoff still comes out of your proceeds.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Carver County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Timeline for a sale

Here is a rough order for a Carver County owner who plans to sell. Months before listing, read the March value notice and decide whether the number is fair. Weeks before listing, ask Property Tax for a balance. At the closing table, expect the title company to prorate the current year and to pay anything overdue out of your proceeds. After closing, the buyer should contact the assessor about homestead so the classification is correct for the next assessment year.

Skipping a lender does not skip any of this. A cash sale still uses the same statement, the same payoff and the same homestead reset.

Local market context

The county spans 354 square miles of land. Population is 114,379, up from 106,922 in 2020, and there are 44,930 housing units. Chaska is the seat of government and the biggest city. Chanhassen lies partly in Hennepin County, so confirm which county bills a Chanhassen parcel before you call.

  • Typical home value: $453,600
  • Median household income: $125,946

Read the March value notice line by line. The date of your local board meeting is printed on it.

Frequently asked questions

What is the May deadline in Carver County?

May 15 for most properties. A statement mailed after April 24 pushes that date to 21 days after the postmark. The October installment falls on October 15, or on November 15 for most agricultural land.

Which Carver County number answers valuation questions?

Call the Carver County assessor at (952) 361-1960 or write to assessment@carvercountymn.gov. The assessor can explain the valuation notice and tell you the board dates for your city or township.

When can I take a Carver County value to Tax Court?

The filing deadline is April 30 of the taxes-payable year. You may file there directly without going to the local or county board first.

What if I mail my Carver County tax payment late?

Penalty begins the next day. If the envelope carries a U.S. postmark within one business day of the deadline and you have never used the abatement before, state law lets the treasurer waive it.

Does the buyer keep my homestead on a Carver County house?

No. The assessor removes the homestead classification for the following assessment year unless the buyer files a homestead application and qualifies. A new owner, a trust transfer or a name change needs a fresh application.

Which department bills and collects

The Property Records and Licensing department in the Government Center at 151 4th Street SE, Rochester, runs both the billing side and the valuation side. Questions about a statement go to 507-328-7636, and prior-year delinquent balances go to 507-328-7635. Payment by mail goes to PO Box 6681, Rochester, MN 55903-6681.

The county's property tax FAQ explains the math: tax is the property's value multiplied by the total rate of the district it sits in, and residential homesteads get a market value homestead exclusion. Value and class come from Assessing Services, reached at 507-328-7670 on weekdays.

The department also offers eNoticesOnline, a free service that delivers the tax statement and valuation notice by email in place of paper, with a Pay button that links to the county's payment portal. A statement carries more than the county's share. School district, city or township and special taxing districts such as watersheds all take a cut, along with any tax increment financing diversion and special assessments for street work.

When you call, give the parcel ID or the street address. Staff can then tell you what has been paid, what is still open, and whether any special assessment sits on the parcel. Ask for the balance in writing if you plan to hand it to a title company or a buyer, so everyone works from the same figure.

Olmsted County housing snapshot

Rochester is the county seat and by far the largest city. Stewartville, the second-largest, has about 6,000 residents, and the rest of the county is farmland and small towns such as Byron, Eyota, Oronoco and Dover. School districts include Rochester Public Schools (ISD 535), Byron (531), Stewartville (534) and Dover-Eyota (533).

Population is 166,731, up 2.4% since the 2020 base. There are 74,363 housing units, and 70.6% are owner-occupied. Median owner-occupied value is $331,700, median gross rent is $1,370, and median household income is $95,406.

With values at that level, the same tax rate produces a bigger dollar bill than in lower-priced counties. Landlords and estates holding a house in Rochester or one of the smaller cities should watch the November Truth-in-Taxation notice and the two installment dates to keep cash flow predictable.

Installment dates

Dates follow the property type, and a due date that falls on a weekend moves to the next working day. A postmark on a mailed payment counts.

Olmsted County tax installments for the 2026 tax year
Property typeFirst halfSecond half
Houses, commercial buildings and personal propertyMay 15, 2026October 15, 2026
Agricultural real estateMay 15, 2026November 16, 2026
Manufactured homesAugust 31, 2026November 16, 2026

The Truth-in-Taxation notice that previews next year's tax goes out each November. It can differ from the real bill because it leaves out special assessments and does not reflect referendums. An owner who occupies a property by December 1 can file for homestead for the following year, and the county shows December 15 as the homestead application date.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Olmsted County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Ways to pay

Your parcel ID is required with every form of payment. The county accepts these options:

  • Online by credit card or e-check, at 3.28% for cards and $3.16 for e-checks, for current-year tax only, with a $300,000 ceiling
  • Bank bill pay, which counts as paid on the day the county receives it, often seven to ten days after the bank issues it
  • Automatic withdrawal (ACH), withdrawn May 10 and October 10, or November 10 for agricultural property; not offered on mobile homes
  • In person at the Government Center, or by mail

The county charges $2 for each reprint of a statement at its office. For ACH, sign-up cutoffs fall on April 10 for the first half and September 11 for the second, and a form that misses a cutoff rolls to the next payment cycle. An online payment can take seven to ten business days to clear the bank, so do not wait for the last day.

How to appeal your valuation

Gather an appraisal, a recent sale of a similar house or other evidence, then call the Assessor at 507-328-7670 or visit 151 4th Street SE. The valuation notice goes out in mid-March. If the conversation does not settle it:

  1. Attend the local board of appeal listed on your notice, which begins in mid-April, or the open book meeting if your area uses one. A jurisdiction with no local board goes straight to the county board.
  2. Attend the County Board of Appeal and Equalization, which meets in June. Owners are asked to book a time at 507-328-6001.
  3. Petition the Minnesota Tax Court by April 30 of the year taxes are payable.

Since the 2023 change to Minnesota Statutes 278.01, a petition must be served on the county auditor. Olmsted County accepts service by email at olmcotaxpetitionservice@olmstedcounty.gov, or in person at the County Attorney's Office, 151 Fourth Street Southeast, and issues an acknowledgement.

How tax is split when a house sells

Statements are mailed in late March, and a mid-year buyer receives none, so the county tells new owners to look the bill up online. At closing, tax is prorated: the seller covers January up to the closing date and the buyer covers the rest of the year. A seller who prepaid the full year is reimbursed by the buyer for the buyer's portion.

One quirk affects sellers: an overpayment made at closing can belong to the previous owner, and the county sends any refund to the party that made the payment. The county also mails a homestead application to new owners after a transfer.

Unpaid tax turns delinquent the following year, goes into judgment, and a residential homestead forfeits to the State of Minnesota after three years. Under section 272.12 the auditor must confirm no delinquent tax before a deed is recorded, so any back balance has to be paid off at or before closing.

Before listing, call 507-328-7635 about any prior-year balance and 507-328-7636 about the current year. Hand the numbers to your title company so the payoff is built into the closing statement. A cash sale skips the lender's payoff letter, but the delinquent-tax check at the auditor's desk still applies.

Frequently asked questions

Which Olmsted County second-half dates apply for the 2026 tax year?

October 15, 2026 for most real estate, and November 16, 2026 for agricultural parcels and manufactured homes. Contact 507-328-7636 about any balance.

Which office answers Olmsted County value questions?

Call Assessing Services at 507-328-7670. The office is at 151 4th Street SE in Rochester and stays open weekdays until 4 p.m. Bring recent sales or an appraisal if you plan to dispute the value.

Will I get a tax statement if I buy mid-year in Olmsted County?

No. Statements are mailed in late March and are not sent for mid-year purchases. You can find the bill on the county website or at its office, and not receiving one does not excuse a late payment.

How do I serve a tax court petition on Olmsted County?

Email the petition to olmcotaxpetitionservice@olmstedcounty.gov before the April 30 deadline, or hand it to staff at the County Attorney's Office, 151 Fourth Street Southeast. The county will send back an acknowledgement of service.

Can I set up automatic tax payments in Olmsted County?

Yes for most parcels, but not for mobile homes. Submit the ACH form with a voided check; money comes out May 10 and October 10, or November 10 for agricultural property. A form that misses the cutoff rolls to the next cycle.
