Selling in Mille Lacs County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Mille Lacs County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Mille Lacs County?
We buy Mille Lacs County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Start with the tax office

One combined Property Records and Taxation Office at 635 2nd Street SE in Milaca handles billing, and the Assessor is on the ground floor of the same historic courthouse. About 20,000 tax parcels fall under the county. Every real estate transfer goes through this office, where deed tax or mortgage registry tax is collected and the ownership record is changed.

The office also certifies whether taxes are paid, so it is the first stop for a house, cabin or lake lot. Learn which half-year payment is open, whether any older year is delinquent, and which class the parcel carries. Buyers ask about class, since a lakeshore parcel taxed as seasonal recreational is billed on a different basis than a year-round homestead.

  • Property Records and Taxation: 320-983-8310 for general questions, 320-983-8301 about redemption notices, and 320-983-8304 when the online tax database misbehaves.
  • Assessor: 320-983-8311 or assessor@millelacs.mn.gov for value and class questions.

Mille Lacs County and the lake

Mille Lacs County is in east central Minnesota and takes its name from Mille Lacs Lake. It covers 682 square miles, and about 109 of them, or 16%, are water. The county holds Mille Lacs Kathio State Park, Father Hennepin State Park and part of the Mille Lacs Indian Reservation. Courthouse business happens in Milaca, while Princeton, which extends into Sherburne County, is the biggest city. Isle, Onamia, Foreston, Pease, Bock and Wahkon are the others.

The 2025 estimate is 27,753 people, a 4.8% rise over the 2020 base. In 2020 the county had 12,786 housing units and 17.2% stood vacant, a reminder of how many cabins and seasonal homes are in the mix. For 2020 to 2024, 77.9% of homes were owner occupied and the typical home value was $258,300.

Due dates

Each property type has its own schedule.

  • Real property: May 15 and October 15.
  • Agricultural property: May 15 and November 15.
  • Mobile homes: August 31 and November 15.
  • Personal property: May 15, with one payment.

Real estate and personal property statements go out in March and must be mailed by March 31. Manufactured home statements follow in the first week of July. Each mortgage company gets its own listing, and escrowed owners still receive a statement for their files. A manufactured home parcel stays in the old owner's name until the certificate of title is transferred, and that transfer first requires every current and delinquent personal property tax to be paid.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mille Lacs County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Cabin, farm and home classes

Class sets the rate applied to your value, and the Assessor publishes short definitions. These stand out for the area:

  • Residential homestead (1a): the primary residence of the owner or a qualifying relative.
  • Residential nonhomestead (4b): a home that is the primary residence of someone else, with no more than three livable units.
  • Seasonal recreational residential (4c): a secondary, weekend or vacation home that is no one's primary residence.
  • Seasonal commercial (4c): resorts and other income property open fewer than 250 days a year.
  • Rural vacant land (2b): unplatted, unimproved land of more than five acres.
  • Managed forest (2c): at least 20 unplatted, unimproved acres with a Forest Stewardship Plan.

If a cabin buyer plans to live there year-round, talk through the change early, since homestead status ends at sale and the buyer must apply. For larger tracts, designated public roads are exempt and private roads and driveways are taxable.

When taxes go delinquent

Penalties add up monthly after each due date, yet a tax year is not delinquent until the next January 1. This is the sequence for a parcel that stays unpaid.

Mille Lacs County delinquent tax timeline
DateWhat happens
January 1 after the payable yearThe taxes are classified as delinquent and interest begins to accrue monthly
February 15Parcels still owing go on the delinquent list filed with the court administrator, and the owner is mailed a letter
On or before March 20First newspaper publication of the list
At least two weeks laterSecond publication, with paid parcels removed
Second Monday in MayJudgment is taken and the parcel is bid in for the state
Usually three years afterRedemption period ends in most cases

Someone unable to pay in full can sign a confession of judgment. It folds delinquent tax, special assessments, penalties, costs and interest into a single sum paid over 5 or 10 years, depending on class, and the plan is cancelled if current-year tax lapses. Notices of expiration of redemption are the last step before forfeiture. They go out by certified mail, the sheriff serves them, and the county paper prints them.

How to pay

The online portal finds statements by owner name, parcel ID, street address, or section, township and range. Paying there adds a processor fee: 2.35% on a card, with a $2.00 floor, or $2.00 on an e-check, and the county keeps none of it. Other payments go by mail to the Property Records and Taxation Office, 635 2nd Street SE, Milaca, MN 56353. A declined online payment is a question for your bank. If the database shows an error, try again in 15 minutes and then call 320-983-8304.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mille Lacs County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to appeal a valuation

Your Notice of Valuation and Classification comes in March, at least ten days ahead of the meeting in your township or city. The meeting details are printed at the bottom, and some jurisdictions run open book sessions with the assessor in place of a formal board.

Gather proof such as a recent appraisal or comparable sales, have the Assessor review the data, then present at the local board in April or May in person, through a representative or by letter. Next comes an appointment with the county board in June, open only to owners who made the local appeal first. Anything still unresolved can go to the Minnesota Tax Court, with the petition filed before April 30 of the payable year.

For Tax Court, the county's instructions call for four copies of the petition and five of the tax statement. Serve the Assessor, the County Attorney and the Auditor-Treasurer, then file the original with the court administrator and pay the fee. Expect a trial date within a year.

Tax breaks and refunds

The homestead market value exclusion shrinks the taxable value of a homestead, and so the net tax, and it phases out for higher-value homes. Ask the Assessor for the current figures.

Minnesota also pays an income-based homestead refund. The county does not handle it and sends questions to the Department of Revenue. A Form M1PR claim has to include a tax statement showing no delinquent tax on the homestead. August 15 is the due date, with late returns accepted until August 15 of the following year, and timely claims are paid in late September or early October. The Assessor is also collecting reassessment questionnaires for 2027, the year each property gets its physical review under the five-year cycle.

What a seller settles before closing

Request a payoff for the open half and a certification of paid or unpaid tax from the Property Records and Taxation Office. Under Minnesota Statutes 272.12 a deed is not recorded until the auditor confirms no delinquent taxes and enters the transfer. Sales above $3,000 need a certificate of value (272.115), and homestead status drops off after a transfer until the buyer applies and qualifies.

The Assessor sends a sales verification questionnaire for sales in the county. Verified sales are used to study the market and set values, and the state uses the same studies for refunds and aid payments.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where do I mail a Mille Lacs County tax check?

Send it to the Property Records and Taxation Office, 635 2nd Street SE, Milaca, MN 56353, or pay through the online portal. Call 320-983-8310 with questions.

What are the Mille Lacs County tax due dates?

Real property is due May 15 and October 15, and agricultural property is due May 15 and November 15. Mobile homes are due August 31 and November 15, and personal property is due May 15.

What fees apply when paying Mille Lacs County taxes online?

Cards cost 2.35% with a $2.00 minimum, and e-checks cost $2.00. The processor collects both and the county gets nothing.

Is there an installment plan for back taxes in Mille Lacs County?

Yes. A confession of judgment spreads delinquent taxes, assessments, penalties, costs and interest across 5 or 10 years, provided current-year taxes keep getting paid.

Can I skip the local meeting and go straight to the Mille Lacs County board?

No. The June county meeting is open only after you raise the concern at the local board or open book meeting in April or May. Tax Court petitions are due before April 30.

Who handles property tax in Aitkin County

Responsibility is split. One office sets the value and class of each parcel, and another sends the bills and takes payment. The Assessor's Office answers at 218-927-7327. The Treasurer is at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431, and takes calls at 218-927-7325.

Market value and classification are the main inputs to a tax bill, and the Assessor works under Minnesota statutes, Department of Revenue directives and County Board directives. A free parcel viewer called LINK shows basic parcel data. More detailed building records, including dimensions and sales reports, need a paid subscription, which the Assessor can explain by phone.

A seller will end up talking to both offices: the Assessor about value and class, and the Treasurer about any balance on the parcel before the deed is signed.

Local market snapshot

Aitkin County sits in east central Minnesota, and its seat is the city of Aitkin. Population is 16,252. There are 14,681 housing units, and 85.3% are lived in by their owners. The median value of an owned home is $255,800, and households earn a median $60,833. About 35.7% of residents are past 65, which matters if you are selling a house that belonged to a relative. Much of the county is wooded, and 214 building permits were issued in 2025.

The 2027 reassessment

The county is inspecting properties in a set of areas for its 2027 reassessment, with appraisers on the road since May 2026. An inspection can land anywhere through February 2027, so yours may still be ahead.

The areas are Ball Bluff, Balsam, Fleming, Hazelton, Jevne, Macville, Malmo and Turner townships, unorganized territories 51-22, 52-24 and 52-25, and the city of Hill City. It is a physical inspection used to check and fix county records, and state law calls for it on all taxable property at least every five years.

Owners who want to be there for the walk-through can phone 218-927-7327, and the office also asks to hear about any hazards to avoid on the land. If you are in one of these areas, keep receipts for recent repairs handy.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Aitkin County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal a valuation or classification

The county sets a sequence, and the first step is a phone call.

  • Contact the Assessor's Office with the front and back of your valuation notice in front of you.
  • Next comes the local board of appeal, staffed by the township board or city council, or an Open Book session if that is what your notice lists. At Open Book, the assessors review the case and decide, and that decision can still go to the county board.
  • After that is the county board, which meets in June. You schedule a time through the County Assessor. The local step comes first unless your area has no local board.
  • The last stop is the Minnesota Tax Court, which accepts petitions even from owners who skipped the earlier steps. The deadline is April 30 of the taxes-payable year.

Statute 274.01 puts local board meetings in April and May and caps their combined reductions at one percent of the assessor's total. Under 278.01, an owner may instead serve a petition on the county auditor and file it in district court.

Due dates and penalties

Bills come in two installments, one in mid-May and one in mid-October.

Aitkin County payment rules
Payment stepRule that applies
First halfDue before May 16
Second halfDue before October 16, with no second-half statement mailed
Mailed paymentOn time when the postmark shows the due date or earlier
Late penalty after the due date2% on homestead, 4% on nonhomestead
Delinquent statusTax still unpaid when the new year begins
Delinquent listPrinted in the newspaper each March

The Treasurer does not mail second-half statements, so keep the stub from the first one. Missing paperwork is no defense, because the owner is still responsible, and courtesy letters for unpaid current-year tax carry added penalty and fees. After the first jump, the statute adds one percent per month, up to 8% on homestead and 12% on nonhomestead land.

A tax of $100 or less is due in one payment with the first half. Owners of small parcels should ask the Treasurer which threshold applies before paying.

Selling with taxes owed

Delinquent taxes get paid at closing. The closing statement, or the realtor or attorney on the deal, will show how the current year is divided. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff amount well ahead of the closing date.

Escrow customers have a lender that receives the figures straight from the county. The copy mailed to the owner says in bold print not to pay, yet it remains useful at filing time and for refund claims. A buyer who closes after statements went out can get a copy online or from the Treasurer, and getting it is the buyer's job.

Two state rules touch the deed itself. Statute 272.115 requires a certificate of value on sales above $3,000 and has the assessor remove homestead status after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies. Statute 287.21 sets the deed tax at 0.33% of net consideration above that figure.

A mobile home is handled separately. Its title cannot move until the taxes are paid, and relocating one takes a Mobile Home Clearance Sheet from the Treasurer.

A short checklist before you list: get the current parcel balance from the Treasurer, find your first-half stub, confirm your homestead status with the Assessor, and ask whether your area is in the reassessment. With those four items in hand, the closing agent can work faster and your settlement statement holds fewer surprises.

A cash sale skips the lender's escrow and payoff steps, but the tax balance still has to be cleared from proceeds at closing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Aitkin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Tax relief programs

Homeowners here can look at two programs. The state property tax refund is claimed on form M1PR, available from the Department of Revenue.

The second is the Senior Citizen Property Tax Deferral. It is a low-interest loan from the state, not tax forgiveness. Homeowners aged 65 or older with household income of $60,000 or less can defer part of the tax, the state pays the county, and interest accrues. A seller already in the program should ask the Department of Revenue how a sale affects the deferred balance before listing.

If you cannot tell whether either program fits, the Treasurer at 218-927-7325 can say what to bring.

Frequently asked questions

Which office answers questions on an Aitkin County tax bill?

The Treasurer, at 218-927-7325, handles billing, payments and statement copies, from an office at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119. For value or class questions, dial the Assessor at 218-927-7327.

Does Aitkin County accept mailed tax payments?

Yes. A payment counts as timely if the postmark meets the due date. Address it to the Treasurer at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431. The back of each stub has a form for changing the mailing address.

What if my Aitkin County tax statement never arrives?

You still owe the tax and the same penalties apply. A replacement copy can be printed online or requested from the Treasurer.

Must back taxes be cleared to close an Aitkin County sale?

Yes, delinquent taxes are paid at closing. Tax left unpaid into the next calendar year is delinquent, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff amount well ahead of the closing date.

Can I contest my value after the spring boards adjourn?

Yes, by petitioning the Minnesota Tax Court before April 30 of the taxes-payable year. The court hears owners who never went to the local or county board.

Becker County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Becker County?

Which offices run property tax

Becker County divides the job between the Assessor and the Auditor-Treasurer. The Assessor is appointed by the County Board of Commissioners and approved by the Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue. That office supervises assessments for every township and city in the county and keeps records on about 29,200 taxable properties and 3,339 tax-exempt ones.

Appraisal work is done by state accredited and certified staff from the county office, along with certified assessors hired by townships and cities. The county supplies value and classification schedules built from sales ratio studies, and the Assessor uses them to equalize values between properties, taxing districts, school districts and neighboring counties.

The Auditor-Treasurer, an elected official, calculates rates, prepares statements and Truth in Taxation notices, collects the tax and county special assessments, and tracks unpaid parcels. Most Assessor records are public, apart from data covered by the privacy act.

Local market context

Becker County is in northwest Minnesota, with Detroit Lakes as the county seat. The county mixes farmland, forest and several hundred lakes, among them Detroit Lake, Lake Sallie, Lake Maud, Lake Melissa and Big Cormorant Lake. Population is 35,497, and there are 20,440 housing units, with 77.2% lived in by the owner. An owned home has a median value of $291,000, and median rent is $920. Monthly owner costs run $1,691 with a mortgage and $580 without.

Assessment calendar

These are the dates a homeowner is most likely to need.

  • January 2 is the assessment date for real and personal property.
  • February 1 is the last day to file for exemption from taxation.
  • March 31: statements go out by this date from the Treasurer, except for manufactured homes.
  • April 1 to May 31: local boards of appeal and equalization hold their meetings, and value notices go out at least ten days ahead.
  • April 30: last day to file a Tax Court petition about current taxes.
  • June: the County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets during the last ten meeting days after the second Friday, with times printed on the valuation notice.
  • August 15: deadline for the Property Tax Refund, Form M-1PR.
  • Late November: Truth in Taxation notices go out, with public hearings in the weeks after.

December 1 is the last day for owners of real property to establish homestead for the year, though applications can be filed with the Assessor until December 15 to count for that year's assessment.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Becker County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

Most owners pay in two installments, May 15 and October 15. Several exceptions depend on property class.

Becker County property tax due dates by property class
DateProperty and installment
May 15First half of real property tax; personal property tax
May 31First half for class 1c and 4c resorts and qualifying class 3a seasonal commercial property
August 31First half of manufactured home personal property tax
October 15Second half for non-farm real property
November 15Second half for farm real property and for manufactured homes

Under Statute 279.01, when statements miss an April 25 postmark, the first installment moves to 21 days after the postmark date. Class 3a seasonal property qualifies for the later date only if the owner attaches an affidavit showing more than 60 percent of gross income comes from May through August.

A homestead owner on federal active service as a National Guard or reserve member gets four extra months. A May 15 payment moves to September 15 and an October 15 payment to February 15, with a copy of orders or form DD214.

Paying online

The Auditor-Treasurer's page links to an online and phone payment service, and e-check or card payments through it carry extra fees. You need specific identifiers so the payment is credited to the right parcel.

  • Bill number: five digits, leaving off the beginning zero, printed on the first-half and second-half stubs.
  • Parcel or property ID: all nine digits with no decimal points, so 01.0001.000 is entered as 010001000.
  • Jurisdiction code: 3308 identifies Becker County.

The same page offers a parcel and tax record search showing taxes, assessments, and land and building features, linked to the county's online mapping. Run it before you list to review what is on record for your parcel.

How to appeal your value

Begin with the Assessor, because a conversation about the value notice often resolves a data error. If it does not, the local board is the next step. Statute 274.01 makes the town board or city council the local board unless the city has a charter board or has handed the job to the county. Someone who ignores a notice that the board plans to raise the assessment generally cannot go to the county board later.

The county board convenes in June. After that, a petition to district court or Tax Court under Statute 278.01 must be on file by April 30 of the taxes-payable year. Appeals of manufactured homes assessed as personal property run on a separate calendar, with a September 1 petition date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Becker County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

The Auditor-Treasurer touches the sale before the Recorder does. That office collects the state deed tax, mortgage registration tax and split fees on conveyances and enters each transfer in a permanent database before the document is filed with the County Recorder. Questions on the electronic certificate of real estate value go to the Assessor's chief deputy.

Before you list, gather three things: your latest value notice, your last tax stubs and the parcel ID. With those, the Assessor can check your classification and homestead status, and the Auditor-Treasurer can tell you exactly what is owed on the parcel. Sellers with a resort, farm or seasonal property should also confirm which due dates in the schedule above apply to them, since the class decides the date.

Unpaid tax carries consequences beyond penalties. The Auditor-Treasurer puts delinquent parcels into judgment, runs forfeiture proceedings and sales under statute, and may use revenue recapture to collect. If you owe a back balance, settle it before closing instead of leaving it for the buyer's title company to find. In a cash sale the same balance comes out of your proceeds at the closing table.

A few programs affect timing. Senior citizens apply for the state's property tax deferral by July 1 for taxes payable the following year, and farmland owners file for Green Acres deferral by May 1. Resort owners declare class 1c or 4c status with the Assessor by January 15, and people who are blind or permanently and totally disabled apply to the Department of Revenue for the special homestead class by October 1.

Frequently asked questions

Who appoints the Becker County Assessor?

The County Board of Commissioners appoints the Assessor, and the Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue approves the appointment. The office supervises assessments for all townships and cities in the county.

When is the second Becker County property tax payment due?

October 15 for non-farm real property. Second-half tax on farm real property, including split-class parcels that are partly agricultural, is due November 15, as is the second half for manufactured homes.

Do Becker County resorts pay property tax on a different date?

Yes. Class 1c and 4c resort property and qualifying class 3a seasonal commercial property may pay the first half by May 31 instead of May 15.

What do I need to pay Becker County taxes online?

You need the five-digit bill number from your payment stub, the nine-digit parcel number without decimal points, and the jurisdiction code 3308. E-check and card payments add fees.

Where do I send questions about a Becker County eCRV?

Contact the Chief-Deputy Assessor, who handles tax estimates, agricultural questions and eCRV inquiries. The County Assessor handles exempt questions and sales inquiries.

Where to go with property tax questions

Property tax business happens at the Renville County Courthouse, 500 East DePue Avenue, Olivia. The Auditor-Treasurer is in Suite 202 (320-523-2071) and calculates and collects tax. The Assessor's office is in Suite 205 (320-523-3645) and runs property records and taxpayer services. Both open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Payments can also be left in the drop box by the courthouse's north door at any hour. The Auditor-Treasurer deals with 27 township boards, 10 city councils and nine school districts, which is why that desk can sort out who levies what on your parcel.

Housing in Renville County

Farming dominates this stretch of the Minnesota River valley, and Olivia is the seat. The county lost 2.5% of its people between April 2020 and July 2025 and now counts 14,356. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $163,200, and 80.2% of households own. Rent runs $790 at the median across 6,056 households. Builders took out only ten permits in 2025, and 23.9% of residents are 65 or older.

Before you list, ask the Assessor how your notice value stacks up against nearby sales, and bring photos of condition problems an appraiser may have missed.

When are Renville County property taxes due?

Real estate tax splits into two payments. May 15 is the first. The second is October 15 for residential property and November 15 for agricultural property. In a year when November 15 is a weekend day, check with the Auditor-Treasurer on whether a Monday payment is still timely.

Renville County real estate tax due dates
Property classFirst halfSecond half
ResidentialMay 15October 15
AgriculturalMay 15November 15

Under Minnesota Statutes section 279.01, a bill of $100 or less is all due on the first date. If you mail a payment and the postmark lands within one business day after a deadline, you can get the penalty abated once, provided you have not used that relief before.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Renville County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the assessor values your home

Every property in the county must be inspected by an appraiser at least every five years, who notes anything that moves market value, such as quality, condition, age and size. Each spring you receive a mailed notice listing the estimated market value from January 2 of this year, the value a year earlier and the classification. Next year's tax is figured from the value on that notice.

Homestead classification lowers the taxable value and requires paperwork:

  • The home must be yours, your main residence, and you must be a Minnesota resident.
  • Every owner who lives there signs the application and gives a Social Security number, as does a resident spouse who is not on the title.
  • ITIN holders can claim homestead too, and the Assessor's office posts that notice in English and Spanish.
  • A farm owner of at least 40 acres who lives within four cities or townships of the land can qualify for an agricultural homestead by actively farming it.

How to appeal your valuation

Phone the Assessor first. After that, take your case to the board that serves your township or city. Township boards meet in early April at halls around the county, and the City of Olivia board meets in April in the evening at Olivia City Hall. The county posts the schedule in February.

A town or city may hand its board duties to the county (section 274.13), and the county then has to offer another way to review values, such as open book meetings in April and May. Open book sessions take place at the Assessor's office, and a recent one served fourteen townships and nine cities. Miss the spring window and you can still petition the district court or Tax Court under section 278.01, no later than April 30 of the tax year.

Unpaid tax and forfeited land

Whatever is unpaid when January starts becomes delinquent, and section 279.02 immediately adds 2% of the original amount. The Auditor-Treasurer's office also runs forfeited land proceedings and posts notices of expiration of redemption.

If a forfeited parcel brings more at auction than is owed, the leftover is surplus: what remains after taxes, penalties, interest and costs. The former owner has six months from the mailing of the notice to claim it. Forfeited parcels sold over the counter must be paid in full with a personal, cashier's or certified check or a money order made out to Renville County.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Renville County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

New construction tax relief

The Auditor-Treasurer administers a Tax Abatement Building Incentive Program meant to encourage new residential construction and the replacement of run-down houses. Call 320-523-2071 for the eligibility rules before you plan a teardown or a new build. A buyer weighing a lot with an old house on it may ask about this program, so know the answer before you list.

Seller checklist before closing

Before you sign a purchase agreement, go down this list.

  • Ask the Auditor-Treasurer what is owed on the parcel and whether any special assessment, such as a ditch assessment, is attached.
  • Look up the parcel and your statement in the county's online property tax portal.
  • Confirm your homestead status and that the value on your spring notice is correct.
  • Expect the county auditor to certify that no delinquent tax exists before the deed is recorded, as section 272.12 requires.
  • File the certificate of real estate value for any sale above $3,000, as section 272.115 requires.

A cash buyer skips lender escrow and payoff steps, though the auditor certification and the certificate filing still apply. Send your payoff figure to the title company early so it lands on the closing statement.

If you owe tax when you list

You can sell with a balance due, but it must be paid off before the deed is recorded. Begin by calling 320-523-2071 and asking what is owed for this year and any earlier one, and whether the second half is open. Ask whether a ditch or other special assessment sits on the parcel, since those show up at transfer too.

Then give the number to your title company, which takes the balance out of your sale proceeds and pays the county so the auditor can certify the parcel. If a lender collects tax through escrow, find out what will be refunded after payoff. Keep each receipt with your closing papers. If the parcel includes farm land, mention that too, because the second half on agricultural property falls a month later than on a house and the payoff depends on which halves are paid.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the second-half date for Renville County farmland?

It is November 15. If that date falls on a weekend, call the Auditor-Treasurer at 320-523-2071 and confirm that the next Monday is accepted before you wait.

Can I pay my Renville County tax after hours?

Yes. Use the drop box by the courthouse's north door in Olivia, which never closes. Or pay at the Auditor-Treasurer's counter when the office is open.

Which board hears appeals for a house in Olivia?

Olivia's own local board of appeal and equalization, which sits at Olivia City Hall at 6 p.m. in April. Call the Assessor at 320-523-3645 for the date.

Can I claim homestead in Renville County with an ITIN?

Yes. The Assessor's office takes homestead applications from ITIN holders. Call 320-523-3645 or stop in, and plan to list each owner living in the home.

How long can a former owner claim surplus after a Renville County tax forfeiture sale?

Six months, counted from the day the surplus notice is first mailed. A claim form comes with the certified-mail notice. Call 320-523-2071 with questions.

Rice County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Rice County, MN Property Tax Guide sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Rice County?

Which office handles what

Payments go to the county's Property Tax & Elections Office, upstairs in the Government Services Building at 320 Third St. NW, Faribault. Its phone is 507-332-6104. Valuation questions go to the Assessor's Office at 507-332-6102.

The counter takes cash, checks and money orders only, so cards must be used online or by phone. The Recorder handles the deed after a sale from the same building, and the county's Beacon site lets you search parcels and print your property tax statement.

Housing market snapshot

Rice County had 69,939 residents in July 2025. Owner-occupied homes had a median value of $320,200 for 2020 to 2024, and 76.3% of homes are lived in by their owners. Median owner costs run $1,922 a month with a mortgage, and median gross rent is $1,083. Faribault and Northfield are the two largest cities, and Northfield crosses into Dakota County, so check which county your parcel is in.

Due dates and penalties

Most houses and other non-farm real estate are billed in two halves, May 15 and October 15. Agricultural property and mobile homes have a later second half, due November 15.

Rice County property tax installments
Property type1st installment2nd installment
Real property, non-agriculturalMay 15Oct. 15
Real property, agriculturalMay 15Nov. 15
Personal propertyMay 15None
Mobile homeAug. 31Nov. 15

A yearly total of $100 or less, or $50 or less for a mobile home, must be paid in full on the first date. Section 279.01 sets the late charge for a missed deadline at 2% of the unpaid amount on homestead land and 4% on nonhomestead land. The same amount is added again on the first of the following month. After that, 1% accrues each month through December, until the total reaches 8% for homestead or 12% for everything else.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Rice County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay and what it costs

No fee applies when you pay by e-check or straight from a checking or savings account. Your options:

  • Online through the Pay Property Taxes page: a 2.4% convenience fee with a $2 minimum applies to credit cards, and $4 to Visa debit.
  • By phone at 1-877-690-3729, using jurisdiction code 3321 and your property ID number. Wait for the confirmation number or the payment does not complete.
  • A quarterly or semiannual ACH plan, with enrollment forms on the county website.
  • By mail, with your check and payment stub, to the Property Tax & Elections Office at 320 Third St. NW, Faribault, MN 55021.
  • Through your lender's escrow account, if taxes are part of your mortgage payment.

How the county values your home

Values are set as of January 2. Each year the Assessor compares its estimates with what homes actually sold for, and the Minnesota Department of Revenue expects the estimates to fall between 90% and 105% of real market value. A house still under construction on January 2 is taxed on whatever share was built by then.

Each March the county mails two papers. One is a Notice of Valuation and Classification, which sets the next year's tax. The other is the current tax statement, which lists each taxing body and county fees. The solid waste service fee is $60 for any parcel with a building valued at $5,000 or more. Owners of several buildings or units pay $60 for each, and commercial buildings use a formula the county board approved.

How to appeal your valuation

Contact the Assessor at 507-332-6102 first. The county holds an open book meeting each April at the Government Services Building, where owners can talk one on one with an assessor, and many issues get settled there. Rice County's three local boards of appeal, for Forest, Shieldsville and Wells Townships, meet in April as well. If your township has its own board, the appeal begins there and only then can go up to the county board.

The County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets in June in the Commissioners Room. Under section 274.13 this board cannot lower the countywide total by more than one percent. If you think the valuation is right, you do not need to attend anything. Your notice lists every appeal option for your jurisdiction, so read it before you call.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Rice County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

The parcel goes to the buyer, yet any unpaid balance stays your responsibility. If tax is still unpaid after the first business day of January, section 279.02 adds 2% and the parcel counts as delinquent. Under section 272.12 the Recorder can then refuse your deed until the auditor certifies nothing delinquent remains. For that reason a Rice County closing normally includes a payoff of whatever remains.

Northfield and Dennison cross county lines, so confirm which county your parcel sits in before choosing an office. The county named on your tax statement tells you which offices apply. A cash buyer can close on a short timeline, but the same payoff still comes out of your proceeds at the table, so get the balance early.

Steps before closing

Give yourself roughly four weeks. Open your parcel on Beacon and check the name and mailing address. Then phone 507-332-6104 for the paid and unpaid amounts, and hand that balance to the title company so it lands on the settlement statement.

At the table, whatever is still owed usually comes out of your proceeds and goes to the county. Paying early on your own works too: choose e-check, which is free, and save the confirmation number. After the deed is recorded, the Recorder's office in the same building finishes the transfer, and the buyer is responsible for the next statement. Anyone planning to sell for cash can move faster than a lender-financed buyer, but taxes still need to be settled before the deed is accepted.

What a Rice County seller should prepare

  • Print the latest statement from Beacon and mark which halves are paid.
  • Call 507-332-6104 if your mailing address has changed or a statement never arrived.
  • Compare your valuation notice with what similar homes sold for, because it sets next year's tax.
  • Ask whether the $60 solid waste fee appears for each building on the parcel.
  • Pick a payment method early, since the counter cannot take cards.

Bring the statement and a photo ID if you visit the counter, and ask the staff for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What does it cost to pay Rice County property tax by credit card?

A 2.4% convenience fee, with a minimum of $2. Visa debit carries a flat $4 fee, and e-check payments have no fee. Cards work online or at 1-877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 3321.

Can I pay with a card at the Rice County counter?

No. The Property Tax & Elections counter takes cash, checks and money orders only. For a card, pay online or use the phone line.

What is the $60 fee on my Rice County statement?

It is the solid waste service fee, charged on parcels with a building valued at $5,000 or more. It funds recycling, household hazardous waste, composting and waste reduction. Owners of several units pay $60 per unit.

Where do I appeal if my Rice County township has no local board?

Call the Assessor at 507-332-6102 and attend the open book meeting, then the County Board of Appeal and Equalization. Your valuation notice lists every appeal option for your jurisdiction.

Is another Rice County property tax payment due after October 15?

Only for agricultural property and mobile homes, whose second half is due November 15. Regular real estate is done after October 15, and the next first half comes in May.

St. Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • St. Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is

Selling in St. Louis County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in St. Louis County?
We buy St. Louis County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which office bills St. Louis County property tax?

The Auditor sends the bills while the Assessor sets the values. The county is huge, with Duluth as the seat, and that two-city layout shows up in services. The Auditor's office works from the Duluth Courthouse, the Mall-Service Center and the Government Services Center in Virginia, and property tax payments alone can also be made at the Hibbing Courthouse through the County Recorder.

The Tax Division is at 100 N. 5th Ave. W. in Duluth, phone 218-726-2383. The Assessor's job is market value and classification. That office does not collect taxes, calculate them, set rates or write property tax law, so send billing questions to the Tax Division.

Housing in St. Louis County

Homes here are modestly priced and the headcount is steady. July 2025 population was 200,518, almost level with the 200,227 counted at the April 2020 base. There are 105,503 housing units and 87,115 households, with 71.2% owner-occupied. Owned homes sit at $221,400 in the middle, and middle gross rent is $1,013. With only 32 residents per square mile of land, a parcel's location inside the county shapes its value and its tax, which is one reason the assessment and appeal steps below matter to a seller.

Due dates

Real estate and personal property tax split into May 15 and October 15 payments. Farmland waits until November 15 for its second half, and resort property's first half runs to May 31. Weekend deadlines roll to Monday, and a mailed check needs a postmark no later than the deadline.

Statements go out in March, and state law sets March 31 as the cutoff. If none shows up, the owner has to ask the Tax Division for a duplicate. The office never forwards mail, so a returned statement just comes back to Duluth. Partial payments are welcome and are applied first to that year's accrued penalty.

  • E-check payments online through Paymentus are free, and the Auditor's page lists the other methods with their fees.
  • Drop boxes at county locations take checks or money orders, but no cash.
  • A Truth-in-Taxation notice arrives in November and shows the proposed tax for next year, with dates for local budget meetings.

Watch for scam videos claiming a "Senior Homeowner Tax Review Request" tied to a federal law change. The programs and forms they describe do not exist. Real state programs are explained at 218-726-2304.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your St. Louis County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal a St. Louis County valuation

First speak with your assessor, then work through up to three levels in order, unless you go straight to Minnesota Tax Court.

  1. City or township Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, which meets in April or May and can change your value or class. Contact the clerk to appear, or send a letter to the clerk to be read at the meeting. The meeting date is the deadline.
  2. County Board of Appeal and Equalization, in the last two weeks of June, made up of members with extensive real estate knowledge. Book a slot through the Clerk of the County Board at 218-726-2385.
  3. Minnesota Tax Court, with until April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Unorganized townships skip the first level and appeal straight to the county board. The Tax Court has a Small Claims Division for homesteads of any value, other property under $300,000 in market value, and disputes of $5,000 or less including penalty and interest. The Regular Division hears everything else and follows civil procedure rules, so most owners there hire a lawyer. St. Louis County accepts service of Tax Court petitions in person or by email, and the petitioner must file with the district court on time.

What happens if the tax is not paid?

The path is slow but firm. Tax left unpaid becomes delinquent on the first business day of January, and for a homestead the whole process generally takes up to three years.

Steps after St. Louis County property tax goes delinquent
StepTiming
DelinquencyFirst business day of the year after the tax was due
NoticesTwo newspaper notices, the first by March 20, plus a mailing to the owner
Contest window20 days from the second notice to contest in District Court
Judgment and saleJudgment entered in May, tax judgment sale on the second Monday in May
Redemption3 years for homestead property under the 2014 rule
ForfeitureWhen redemption ends or 60 days after the last warning, whichever is later

Paying all delinquent tax and fees before redemption ends stops the process. The payment plan is called a confession of judgment. The owner pays one tenth of the delinquent tax, penalties and fees plus the current year's tax, and then pays the rest over up to 10 years for a homestead. After forfeiture the owner may be able to repurchase, but there is no guarantee, and the owner receives none of the proceeds if the county sells the land.

Tax steps when you list a house

Call the Tax Division at 218-726-2383 and request the current balance, including penalty and any special assessment, well ahead of closing. Special assessments for improvements such as streets appear on the statement as a separate amount, and they are based on the benefit to the property, not its value.

Some parcels here have extra layers. Tax Increment Financing districts divert part of the tax to the district without changing how the bill is figured, and fiscal disparities share a portion of commercial and industrial growth with the seven-county metropolitan area. If a buyer or title company asks about either, the Auditor's Tax Division can say whether a parcel is affected.

A Mortgage/Deed Tax Calculator is linked from the Auditor's page. The Recorder's office notes that property in the county is either Abstract or Torrens title, which affects how documents are recorded. For legal advice or help drafting documents, go to a real estate attorney or a practicing abstractor. Ask the Recorder which title type applies to your parcel before the deed is prepared.

If you sell for cash, none of this changes. The balance still has to be paid at closing, so a quick call to the Tax Division before you accept an offer lets you plan around the payoff. Bring the parcel number from your statement, and ask whether any special assessment is still running so nothing surprises you at the table.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy St. Louis County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What are the St. Louis County tax deadlines?

May 15 for the first half and October 15 for the second half of real estate and personal property tax. Agricultural second halves are due November 15, and the postmark must show the due date or earlier.

How do I book a hearing before the St. Louis County board of appeal?

Call the Clerk of the County Board at 218-726-2385. The County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets in the last two weeks of June, after the city or township board has acted.

Is there a free way to pay St. Louis County tax?

Yes, e-check payments through Paymentus are free. Other online methods carry fees listed on the Auditor's page, and checks or money orders (no cash) can go in a county drop box.

What is the redemption period for a delinquent St. Louis County homestead?

Three years for homestead property under the rule effective in 2014. You may pay all delinquent tax and fees at any time before redemption ends, or enter a confession of judgment payment plan.

Where does an unorganized township owner appeal in St. Louis County?

Directly to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization, because those townships have no local board. Call the Clerk of the County Board at 218-726-2385 to book a time.

Which Steele County office do I call about my tax bill?

Call the Property Tax and Elections office at 507-444-7410 for the tax calculation and records, and the Finance office at 507-444-7420 for payments. Both work from the County Administration Building at 630 Florence Avenue in Owatonna, and mail goes to P.O. Box 890, Owatonna, MN 55060. The Assessor's Office, at 507-444-7435, handles value and classification.

The Property Tax and Elections page describes what that office does: it works out the tax capacity rates, computes the tax on each parcel from the budgets of the county, townships, cities and school districts, assigns special assessments, processes deed transfers and keeps delinquent tax records. It also runs Confession of Judgment contracts for owners behind on a bill, handles county ditch records and collects the aggregate tax.

The county mails real estate statements each March and mobile home statements each July. Every owner gets a statement, including owners whose lender pays through escrow, so a seller should be able to find the current one.

Housing in Steele County

Steele is a small, mostly agricultural county in southern Minnesota with Owatonna as its seat and largest city. Population was 37,464 in July 2025, barely changed since 2020. Owners live in 79.4% of homes, the median owner-occupied value is $245,400, and median gross rent is $1,061. Only 54 building permits were counted last year. Sellers here may have a town lot, acreage inside township lines or a farmstead, and each has a different local board, a different set of special assessments and sometimes a different tax class.

Due dates

Real estate tax is due in two halves. Agricultural second-half tax is due November 15, and a weekend date rolls forward to the following business day, which puts this year's farmland payment on Monday, November 16. Confirm that date with the Finance office if you own farmland.

Steele County payment dates
DateWhat is due
January 1Unpaid tax from the prior year becomes delinquent
May 15First half real estate
August 31First half mobile home
October 15Second half real estate
November 15Second half agricultural

The drop box in front of the Administration Building takes payments until 8:00 a.m. on the business day after the due date. After that hour the payment must include the penalty.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Steele County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay a Steele County tax bill

You can pay in person, by mail, at the drop box, by card or e-check, or through direct debit. The Finance office is on the first floor of the Administration Building and keeps weekday business hours.

  • In person at 630 Florence Avenue, Owatonna, on weekdays except federal holidays.
  • By mail to Steele County Finance, P.O. Box 890, Owatonna, MN 55060.
  • Online or by phone through the Tax Information and Parcel Data link. The fees are 2.5 percent of the tax, with a $1.50 minimum, for a credit or debit card, $3.95 flat for a Visa debit card, and $1.50 for an e-check under $10,000 or $10.00 above that.
  • Direct debit in two installments with no convenience fee. Forms are due in the Finance office by April 30 for the spring half and September 30 for the fall half.

Save the confirmation of any electronic payment, since the county asks owners to keep it.

Where does a Steele County owner take a value dispute?

Talk to the Assessor's appraiser first, then appear before the local board of appeal and equalization, then the county board if needed. Township boards meet in April, and open book sessions are held in Blooming Prairie, Medford and at the Administration Building around the same time. The county board meets in June in the evening. Your valuation notice lists the current dates.

A reduction has to be backed by facts, because a lower value moves tax onto other property. The assessor values each parcel as of January 2 at its usual selling price under Minnesota Statutes 272.03. The county's property tax programs page lists the special agricultural homestead, the market value exclusion for owners with a disability, the special homestead for blind or disabled owners, Green Acres and Rural Preserve, exempt property and a senior deferral.

Selling with tax owed

Unpaid tax turns delinquent every January 1 after its due year, and a parcel with delinquent tax may not be transferred. That means a balance has to be cleared before a deed can be recorded. Call the Property Tax and Elections office at 507-444-7410 for the payoff, and ask whether a Confession of Judgment contract is open on the parcel, since that office runs those contracts for owners who are behind.

A cash buyer will still expect the title to be clean, so the same steps apply. Get the balance, pay it from the proceeds at closing or before, and ask the Recorder's Office at 507-444-7450 to confirm the deed has what it needs before you sign.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Steele County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What Steele County requires to record a sale

A deed recorded in Steele County must carry the deed tax, an electronic certificate of real estate value number and a well disclosure. The Recorder's checklist spells out each item for a transfer deed.

  • Deed tax is the purchase price times 0.0033, and the eCRV number goes on the first page when the price is $3,000 or more.
  • The well disclosure certificate costs $54, unless the seller uses one of the two statements the checklist allows.
  • The deed must name where to send tax statements, and grantors must state their marital status.
  • Properties with delinquent taxes may not be transferred.

If you plan to split a parcel before the sale, the county charges $100, requires all current-year taxes paid on every parcel involved, and asks for a survey on rural land under 40 acres. A parcel inside a city also needs that city's approval.

Other Steele County offices to know before closing

Four other county numbers are worth keeping beside the tax statement. The Recorder's Office at 507-444-7450 files the deed and answers questions about the checklist. Planning and Zoning and Environmental Services share 507-444-7475 and cover building permits and land-use rules in the townships. The GIS office at 507-444-7489 maintains the parcel maps, and the Assessor's Office posts an annual calendar and a frequently asked questions sheet for owners.

Ditch assessments are another item that can ride on a rural parcel. The Property Tax and Elections office keeps the county ditch records and files ditch liens and maintenance assessments, so a farm or acreage seller should ask whether the parcel sits in a county drainage system. The same office also collects the aggregate tax and holds the tax-forfeited land process.

For a first conversation, bring the parcel number from your statement. Every one of these offices keys its records to it.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Steele County Assessor's phone number?

507-444-7435. The office is in the County Administration Building at 630 Florence Avenue, Owatonna, and handles value and classification questions.

Does Steele County mail a second-half tax statement?

No. The county mails one real estate statement each March that lists both halves, with special assessments shown on line 13.

Can I use the drop box for Steele County property tax?

Yes. It sits in front of the Administration Building next to the flagpoles, and payments are accepted through 8:00 a.m. the next business day after the due date. Later payments owe a penalty.

What is the deadline for paying delinquent Steele County tax before forfeiture?

Unpaid tax turns delinquent every January 1 after its due year, and the owner then has either one or three years depending on the property's classification. Ask the Property Tax office at 507-444-7410 which applies.

Are any Steele County tax-forfeited properties for sale?

Call 507-444-7410 or stop in at the Administration Center for terms of sale.

Where to go for property tax

You will find both offices in the Itasca County Courthouse, 123 NE 4th Street, Grand Rapids, MN 55744. Weekday service ends at 4:30 p.m., and the Auditor/Treasurer has the second floor. Call the Assessor at 218-327-2861 and the Treasurer at 218-327-2860.

Locating, listing and valuing every taxable parcel is the Assessor's job, along with net tax capacity by class, the value and classification notices, and the local and county boards of equalization. The Auditor/Treasurer mails the statements and takes your money.

Itasca County in brief

Itasca County is wooded lake country in the Iron Range region, and Grand Rapids is the county seat. Only two Minnesota counties are bigger by area. Itasca has 2,668 square miles of land and more than 1,400 lakes, including Winnibigoshish, Pokegama, Deer and Bowstring. The July 2025 estimate is 45,404 residents, only 0.9% above 2020.

There are 26,005 housing units, and 83.0% of occupied homes are owned. The median owner-occupied home is worth $225,200. The 2020 census found 25.2% of housing units vacant, a sign of how many cabins and seasonal places are in the mix. That matters when you list, because a lake property or a seasonal home is taxed under a different class than a house lived in all year.

Who values your house

Valuation for every taxable parcel is done by the Assessor's office, so a seller in a far-flung township such as Bigfork, Marcell or Wawina still begins at the courthouse in Grand Rapids for value and classification questions. Where a city assessor also works in your area, the county assessor passes a copy of any petition to that authority, so ask which office issued your notice.

The value on that notice is as of the assessment date, and it feeds the next tax bill, so a buyer's lender and your title company will both look at it. If it seems off, raise it with the Assessor before you list rather than after an offer comes in.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Itasca County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates

A residential bill splits into May 15 and October 15 payments. Resorts, manufactured homes and agricultural land keep their own dates, and a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday moves any date to the next business day.

Itasca County payment due dates
Due dateTax type
May 15Real property, first half (or whole bill if $100 or less)
May 31Real property, resorts, first half
August 31Manufactured homes, first half (or whole bill if $50 or less)
October 15Real property, second half
November 15Agricultural real property and manufactured homes, second half

Personal property and severed mineral interest taxes come due along with the real property tax.

How to pay an Itasca County tax bill

Four routes exist: mail, the website, the phone line, or the courthouse counter, which accepts cash, check, debit and credit. For mail, the postmark must be on or before the deadline.

  • Cards carry a 2.25% service fee with a $1.00 minimum.
  • An e-check through MuniciPay costs a flat $1.00 per transaction under $100,000.
  • Phone payments go through 218-535-7880 and need the Property ID Number from the top left of the statement.
  • Expect an online or phone payment to post in one to two business days.

Automatic payment enrollment is free, with the same $1.00 ACH fee. Taxes paid out of a mortgage escrow show a do-not-pay note on the statement, and a new escrow agent has to be reported to the Auditor/Treasurer by the escrow company itself.

Late payment penalties

Miss an installment and Minnesota Statutes section 279.01 adds 2% to a homestead bill or 4% to any other. A second charge of equal size follows when the next month begins, and after that the penalty grows by one percent every month until December.

Penalty tops out at 8% for homestead and 12% for nonhomestead property. Farm homesteads and certain rural land get a break on the second half alone, with no penalty through November 15. The treasurer can also forgive one penalty if your mailed check carries a postmark within a business day of the deadline. Cabins and seasonal recreational property that are not used commercially pay the homestead penalty rates, which counts for a lot in a county with this many lake properties.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Itasca County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to challenge your valuation

Your starting point is a conversation with the Assessor, which the office treats as the first stage of an appeal. After that come the local board in your city or township and then the county board. The Assessor speaks for the county if a case reaches tax court.

Still not satisfied? Minnesota Statutes section 278.01 lets you petition district court, as long as the petition is served on the county auditor and filed with the court administrator by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Tax Court is a second option, open from the moment the valuation notice arrives until May 1. A value or class change that reaches you after February 28 gives you 60 days, counted from the mailing date of the notice.

Board schedules change from year to year, so call 218-327-2861 for the current meeting dates.

Steps for an Itasca County seller

Begin with your latest statement and the Property ID Number printed at its top left. That number is what the phone payment line asks for, and it is also what the Auditor/Treasurer needs to look up what is owed. Next, check which date applies to your property. A house follows the May 15 and October 15 pattern, a resort gets May 31 for the first half, and farmland and manufactured homes have their own later dates.

Then decide who pays what. If your lender escrows, the escrow company handles the payment, so ask the lender what happens to the balance after the sale. If you pay directly, a mailed check must be postmarked on time, and an online or phone payment needs a day or two to post, so do not leave it for the last afternoon before a deadline.

Settling taxes before closing

Get a current statement or payoff from the Auditor/Treasurer for your parcel, and confirm whether the first and second halves of the current year are both paid. The county has its own parcel information system and an online statement lookup.

A house at a lake, on forest land or in a township far from Grand Rapids may carry special assessments, so confirm every line with the county office before you set a closing date. For an inherited, empty or delinquent property, bring the parcel number and latest statement and ask what is owed through the date you expect to close. Paying that figure at the table is what lets the deed move forward, and a cash sale does not skip it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When is the Itasca County first half due?

Regular real property pays the first half on May 15. A resort has until May 31, and a weekend or holiday pushes any deadline to the next business day.

What is the card fee for paying Itasca County taxes?

A card costs 2.25% of the payment, with a $1.00 minimum. Choosing the county's online e-check instead costs a flat $1.00 on any transaction under $100,000.

Where is the Itasca County Assessor?

Inside the courthouse at 123 NE 4th Street, Grand Rapids, MN 55744, open weekdays until 4:30 p.m. Call 218-327-2861.

When is the court deadline to contest an Itasca County tax?

A district court petition is due April 30 of the year the tax is payable, per Minnesota Statutes section 278.01. Tax Court is open earlier, from the day the notice arrives until May 1.

Do manufactured homes in Itasca County follow the same calendar?

No. A manufactured home owes its first half on August 31, or the entire bill if it is $50 or less, and the rest on November 15.

Who handles your tax bill

Two county offices share the work in Austin, and both sit in the Government Center at 201 1st Street NE. The Auditor-Treasurer in Suite 7 collects the money and can be reached at 507-437-9535. The Assessor in Suite 10 sets value and class and answers at 507-437-9440, Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM.

The Auditor-Treasurer's office collects real estate, personal property and mobile home taxes, then pays each school district, city, township and special taxing district its share. The same desk collects special assessments that cities and townships levy for water, sewer, sidewalk, curb and gutter, septic and ditch repair.

Mower County runs a "true county assessor" system. County appraisers, not city or township assessors, value all of the roughly 21,300 parcels each year. One phone number covers every address in the county, from Austin to the smallest township.

Before you call, have your parcel number or street address ready. Staff can then pull up the property card, the current value notice and the tax statement, and tell you whether the first half and second half have been paid. Ask for the class of your property too, since homestead and nonhomestead bills carry different penalty rates.

Mower County housing at a glance

Mower County sits on the Iowa line in southeast Minnesota, and Austin is the county seat and largest city. Population is 40,971, up 2.3% from the 2020 base. There are 17,120 housing units, and 77.6% are lived in by their owners. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $185,200, and median gross rent is $927. The county has no natural lakes, so waterfront premiums rarely come into play.

At a median under $200,000, a fixed repair bill or a back-tax balance takes a larger share of the sale price than it would where values run higher. Clear any tax balance early so it does not eat into a modest margin.

Why an appraiser may visit

Several routine programs put appraisers on the road. They wear reflective vests, drive county-branded vehicles, and leave a card if nobody is home.

  • A five-year review of every parcel, normally run between May and September
  • Building permit reviews, done twice a year in November and January
  • Tax abatement inspections on new homes, required by the county's abatement policy
  • Reports of damaged or destroyed buildings, which owners are asked to call in so a structure that is gone stops being valued
  • Value appeals during April to June, which usually call for a full inspection of the property

Because November is a permit month, a recent addition or finished basement may already be on the appraiser's list. The county also hosts a free online parcel viewer that opens a two-page property card, tax statements and value notices for any parcel, searchable by parcel number, name or address. Pull yours up before you list so you know what the county has on file.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mower County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your value

Start with a call to your appraiser before the board date, because a full inspection is normally required to appeal. The valuation notice arrives each spring and sets the value for taxes payable the next year. The steps run in this order:

  • Local board first. A township board hears appeals in the township, with meetings in mid-April. You must appeal to the local board before the county board.
  • Open book instead of a meeting. Cities and some townships use open book, run in person or by phone at the Assessor's Office from April 6 to May 31, 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. Austin city open book goes through the main office line.
  • County Board of Appeal and Equalization. It meets after the second Friday in June, made up of the County Board and the Auditor, and can change value or classification for the current year.
  • Minnesota Tax Court or district court. Under Minnesota Statutes 278.01, the petition must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Only the estimated market value for the current assessment year is appealable, not the tax bill itself. Local boards also work under section 274.01, which caps their combined reductions at 1% of the assessor's total.

Due dates and penalties

Taxes come due in two halves, mid-May and mid-October, with a later November date for qualifying farm land. Penalties follow Minnesota Statutes 279.01.

Mower County payment deadlines and late charges
Payment or penaltyDeadline or rate
First halfPaid before May 16
Second halfPaid before October 16
Qualifying agricultural land, second halfPenalty-free if paid by November 15
Opening penalty2% on homestead, 4% on nonhomestead
Ceiling after monthly additions8% homestead, 12% nonhomestead
Bills of $100 or lessWhole amount due with the first half

A mailed check is on time when the envelope is postmarked by the due date. A first-time late mailer who postmarks within one business day of the deadline can ask the treasurer to abate the penalty.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid current-year tax becomes delinquent on January 2 of the following year. First-year delinquent owners are notified, and the list appears in the newspaper each March while interest keeps running. Call 507-437-9456 for a payoff figure, since the posted delinquent list can lag behind the current month.

After three years of non-payment a parcel can forfeit to the State of Minnesota. The office sends a Notice of Expiration of Redemption with a last chance to pay, and forfeited parcels are later sold at a county auction. Selling before that point is usually simpler than any redemption.

At transfer, Minnesota Statutes 272.12 has the county auditor check for delinquent tax on the land. The recorder will refuse the deed unless the auditor has marked it with the words "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered." A seller who owes back tax has to clear it at or before closing.

A practical order of work: ask the Auditor-Treasurer for a payoff figure, confirm whether the second half is paid, and give that number to your title company or buyer. A cash buyer can skip the lender's escrow and payoff steps, but the county still wants the tax cleared before it enters the transfer.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call in Mower County to pay or ask about a tax bill?

Call the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-437-9535, or 507-437-9456 for delinquent balances. The office is in Suite 7 of the Government Center, 201 1st Street NE, Austin. Questions about value or class go to the Assessor at 507-437-9440.

Does Mower County mail a valuation notice every year?

Yes, the county values all parcels annually and mails a Notice of Valuation and Classification each spring. The notice lists your local board or open book dates. Read both sides before calling your appraiser.

Can I appeal my Mower County property tax directly to the county board?

Not in most cases. You must go to the local board of appeal first, unless your city or township uses open book, in which case the County Board is the next step. The Tax Court is open at any time before April 30.

Will an appraiser inspect my Mower County home before I sell?

Possibly. Five-year reviews run from May to September, permit checks happen in November and January, and appeals usually require a full inspection. Call 507-437-9440 if a card was left on your door.

What does the county do with parcels that stay unpaid for years?

Delinquent parcels are listed each March, and after three years of non-payment they can forfeit to the State of Minnesota. The county then holds a public auction so the land returns to the tax rolls. Owners get a Notice of Expiration of Redemption before that happens.

Pine County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Pine County?
We buy Pine County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
