Which offices handle your bill

Pine County splits the job between two offices. The Assessor (320-591-1632) puts a value and a class on about 32,000 parcels. The Auditor-Treasurer (320-591-1670) works out the tax from the levies of cities, townships, schools and the hospital district, then bills it, collects it and chases what goes unpaid. That office is at 635 Northridge Drive NW in Pine City, and both offices answer phones Monday through Friday, 8:00 to 4:30.

Appraisers are assigned by geography. One handles Clover and Sandstone townships and the cities of Pine City, Sandstone and Sturgeon Lake. Another has Hinckley, Chengwatana and Pokegama townships and the city of Hinckley. A third covers Barry, Crosby, Kettle River, Norman, Ogema and Pine City townships plus Rock Creek. Ask which appraiser holds your parcel before you dial.

Sellers lean on both. The Assessor's technicians process homestead changes and electronic certificates of real estate value after a sale, and the Auditor-Treasurer quotes what is owed against the parcel.

Pine County housing market basics

Pine City is the county seat, and the county has fourteen cities, among them Hinckley, Sandstone, Rock Creek, Askov and Willow River. Population is 30,472, a 5.5% rise over 2020. There are 17,905 housing units, and 81.6% are owner-occupied. Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $239,300, and median household income is $71,146.

Nearly a third of housing units were counted vacant in 2020, which reflects how many cabins and seasonal homes sit on the lake and forest land. If you own one, check how it is classed, since that affects both the rate and what a buyer will pay in tax.

What dates matter on the Pine County tax calendar?

The Assessor keeps a calendar of state-set deadlines. These are the entries that bite hardest for homeowners and people about to sell.

Pine County's tax year at a glance
WhenEvent
Jan. 2Value is fixed as of this day for the coming tax year
By Mar. 31Treasurer mails statements
Apr. 1 through May 31Local boards may hold their appeal meetings
Apr. 30Tax Court petition deadline for value or class disputes
May 15First installment deadline
Late JuneCounty board of appeal, on a date printed in your valuation notice
July 1Values lock for the year
Aug. 15State M-1PR refund claims close
Oct. 15Second installment on non-farm property and special assessments
Nov. 15Second installment for farm land and manufactured homes
Dec. 31Homestead must be in place by this date

A statement that never showed up changes nothing about the due date, and an envelope postmarked on the due date is treated as paid on time.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Pine County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to challenge your value or classification

Start with a phone call and your spring valuation notice. After that the road runs like this:

  • Ring the Assessor at 320-591-1632 and ask the appraiser for your township or city to look at the value or class again.
  • Present your case to the local board. Township boards and city councils may sit anytime from April 1 to May 31.
  • Move up to the county board in the back half of June. Your notice carries the date.
  • Use Minnesota Tax Court if the boards leave the dispute open, filing by April 30 of the payable year.

July 1 is the point where the county treats the year's assessments as closed, and only a statutory exception can reopen them.

Documents beat arguments. Bring a recent appraisal, a signed purchase agreement, or dated photos of roof, foundation or septic problems that an appraiser driving past would miss.

Paying, penalties and delinquency

Mail a check or money order to Pine County Auditor-Treasurer, 635 Northridge Dr NW, Suite 230, Pine City, MN 55063. A drop box faces the courthouse entrance, and no cash goes in it. Other routes are the county's online payment page, an automated phone line at 1-800-272-9829 (enter 3316 when asked for the Pine County code), and the counter. Card and e-check payments pass a service fee to an outside vendor, so check the amount before you pay that way.

Penalties start the day after a deadline. Statute puts the first jump at 2% for homestead and 4% for nonhomestead, with more added monthly. Once December ends, the county adds interest at 10% a year.

If the bill sits, the county follows this sequence:

  • January 1: the balance counts as delinquent.
  • February 15: the parcel lands on a list filed with the court administrator, and the owner gets a letter.
  • By March 20: newspaper publication begins, with a repeat at least two weeks later.
  • Second Monday in May: judgment is entered and the parcel is bid in toward forfeiture, which in most cases leaves three years to redeem.

A confession of judgment turns the delinquent total into a five-year or ten-year payment plan, provided the current year's tax stays up to date.

What a seller should know about taxes at closing

The Treasurer's counter collects current-year tax, deed tax and mortgage registry tax. For delinquent balances call 320-591-1670, and ask for the payoff in writing: web figures can be off for owners on a payment plan.

State statutes shape the recording step. Under 272.12 the auditor must certify that no delinquent tax is owed before a recorder takes the deed. Section 272.115 requires a certificate of value whenever the price tops $3,000, and it has the assessor remove homestead for the following year unless the buyer qualifies. Section 287.21 sets the deed tax at .0033 of the net price above that threshold.

Manufactured homes run separately. A mobile home parcel will not move into the buyer's name until the title is transferred, and the county will not allow a title transfer while current or delinquent personal property tax remains.

For a cash sale the steps are shorter, because no lender payoff or escrow is involved. You still need the payoff figure, the certificate of value and the auditor's clearance.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pine County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Tax breaks and refunds

Homeowners can claim the Minnesota refund on Form M-1PR. The basic refund requires that you owned the home and lived in it on January 2. A separate special refund can follow when the tax on your homestead jumped more than 12 percent in one year. Forms are available from the Department of Revenue, and August 15 is the last filing day.

A few other deadlines on the calendar: October 1 for blind or permanently and totally disabled owners seeking special homestead status, May 1 for Green Acres and managed forest applications, and December 31 for the disabled veteran market value exclusion. Owners who are falling behind should phone the Auditor-Treasurer before forfeiture steps start. One small rule from the county board: overpayments under $5 are not refunded.

Frequently asked questions

Which Pine County office gives a payoff for back taxes?

The Auditor-Treasurer, at 320-591-1670. Staff there calculate delinquent amounts and write confession of judgment contracts. Get the figure in writing, because web balances can be wrong for parcels on a plan.

Which installments does a Pine County homeowner owe each year?

Two: May 15 and October 15 for ordinary real property. Farm parcels and manufactured homes pay their second half on November 15, and manufactured homes pay the first on August 31.

Is it too late to contest a Pine County value in August?

Almost certainly. The county treats assessments as final once July 1 arrives, apart from changes a statute permits. Next year, work through the local board in April or May and the county board in June.

What happens if my Pine County statement is lost in the mail?

You still owe the tax on time. A missing statement is no defense. Pull the parcel up on the county's online property site or ask the Auditor-Treasurer for a duplicate.

How do I claim the Minnesota refund on a Pine County homestead?

File Form M-1PR with the Department of Revenue by August 15. You must have owned and occupied the home on January 2. A larger special refund exists for tax increases above 12 percent.

Where to go in Gaylord for property tax questions

One building handles it all: the courthouse at 400 Court Avenue. The Auditor-Treasurer, on the first floor, mails and collects the bills (507-237-4070, P.O. Box 51, Gaylord, MN 55334). The Assessor, on the second floor, decides each parcel's market value and class (507-237-4078, P.O. Box 532), with counter hours of 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays.

The dividing line is simple: disputes over tax amounts or special assessments go to the Auditor-Treasurer, while value and classification stay with the Assessor. If you cannot print your current value notice or tax statement from the county's online portal, either office will send a copy.

Housing in Sibley County

Small towns and farmland line the Minnesota River here, and Gaylord is both the county seat and its largest city. The July 2025 population estimate is 15,356, up 3.4% from 2020. There are 6,596 housing units, and owners live in 80.8% of the occupied ones. Owned homes sit at $231,900 in the middle of the range, and middle gross rent is $855. Only 28 building permits were issued during 2025, so most sales here involve houses that already exist.

Due dates

Spring and fall carry the main deadlines. Residential and commercial parcels pay in May and October, farmland pays its second half a month later, and the postmark on a mailed payment has to show the due date or earlier. When the date lands on a weekend, the following business day applies.

Payment calendar for Sibley County parcels
Type of taxFirst paymentSecond payment
Residential or commercial real estateMay 15October 15
Agricultural real estateMay 15November 15
Personal propertyMay 15, full amountNone
Mobile homeAugust 31November 15

A real estate bill of $100 or under is due all at once with the first payment, so the second stub is blank, and mobile home bills under $50 are due whole on August 31. Statements are mailed by the end of March each year. Before you list, search the online portal for any balance still open on the parcel.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Sibley County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What ways are there to pay a Sibley County bill?

The county prefers online or mailed payments. Send every stub with a check, because the office takes no responsibility for a parcel left unpaid. Payments are posted by parcel ID number.

  • Card or e-check: cards cost 2.35% of the amount (minimum $1.50) and e-checks cost a flat $1.50. By phone, call 507-237-4070 during the day or 855-414-3916 after hours.
  • Mail: use the envelope that came with your statement. The Postal Service now dates a letter when it receives it, so mail several days early or request a manual postmark at the counter.
  • Drop box: a locked box at the courthouse west entrance is emptied at 8:00 each morning, and earlier deposits count for the previous day.
  • Direct Payment Plan: free withdrawals on May 15 and October 15 or November 15. Enroll about three weeks before a payment date.

You can send a partial amount whenever you like. The whole half remains due on its date, but penalty builds only on the part still unpaid. Returned payments cost $30. Email reminders go out 10 to 14 days before each deadline if you ask, though penalties apply even when a reminder never arrives.

Challenging a Sibley County valuation

The order is local board first, then the county board, then Tax Court. Each value is pegged to January 2. To set it, the Assessor reviews sales from October 1 through September 30 of the prior year, and state guidance wants assessed levels between 90% and 105% of sale price.

  • Local board: townships and cities hold hearings from April 1 to May 31, and the Assessor attends to present data without a vote.
  • Open Book: where a jurisdiction passes its appeal power to the county, you meet the Assessor informally. Failing agreement there, you can go to the county board in June.
  • Tax Court: April 30 is the final day to petition on a dispute that affects the current year's tax.

You have to prove the value is off, since the assessor is presumed correct. Useful proof includes sales of similar homes, a fresh appraisal or contractor repair bids. The local board may move a value up or down or change a class, yet it cannot cut a whole township or city by more than 1%. Decisions usually arrive by mail within 10 days. A spring postcard announces the physical visit every parcel gets at least once in five years.

What happens to homestead status when a house sells?

A seller has 30 days after the sale to notify the Assessor. Moving out, a spouse moving out and a change in marital status trigger the same duty, and skipping the report can bring the correct tax plus an equal penalty.

A buyer who will live in the house files a fresh application by December 31 of the assessment year, ideally right after closing. Drop the form at the Court Avenue courthouse or mail it to P.O. Box 532. Every owner listed needs a Social Security or ITIN number.

Being away does not end homestead by itself. A winter in the south is fine if the house is kept up as a home waiting for you, and a move to a nursing home or assisted living can also preserve it while the house stays maintained. Renting the place out during an absence ends it, and so does claiming a second Minnesota homestead.

Once a house is rented, listed for sale or occupied by anyone but the owner, it is classed non-homestead from the next assessment year.

Mention the December 31 filing date to your buyer early, and remind them that each owner on the deed needs a Social Security or ITIN number ready. Either office at the courthouse can hand over the form, and filing promptly keeps the new owner's first statement classed correctly.

Settling the tax bill at closing

Phone the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-237-4070 and ask what the parcel owes before you accept an offer. One half could be paid with the other still open, and a special assessment may appear as its own line.

Keep the parcel ID and your latest statement handy for the title company. With escrow, the servicer can issue a payoff letter and close the account after the sale. A cash sale has no lender in between, so the closing agent pays off any tax from your proceeds and divides the current year as the contract directs.

Frequently asked questions

Which dates matter for Sibley County real estate tax?

May 15 for the first half, then October 15 for residential and commercial second halves or November 15 for agricultural ones. Personal property is paid whole on May 15, and mobile homes follow August 31 and November 15.

Where can I find the Sibley County Assessor?

On the second floor of the courthouse, 400 Court Avenue, Gaylord, MN 55334. Phone 507-237-4078. The office is open weekdays from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

What fee applies to a card payment of Sibley County tax?

2.35% of the amount, with a $1.50 minimum, on credit or debit cards. An e-check carries a flat $1.50. Mail, the drop box and the Direct Payment Plan avoid those charges.

When will my Sibley County local board of appeal meet?

Sometime from April 1 through May 31, and your valuation notice lists the date. A county board hearing follows in June for anyone still unsatisfied.

Must I report the sale of my Sibley County home to the county?

Yes. Notify the County Assessor within 30 days of the sale. The office at 507-237-4078 can supply the form and answer questions.

Selling in Todd County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Todd County?

Where to go with Todd County property tax questions

For a bill or a payment, see the Auditor-Treasurer in Suite 201 of the Historic Courthouse, 215 1st Avenue South, Long Prairie (320-732-4469). Questions about value and class belong with the Assessor (320-732-4431). Both counters are open weekdays from 8 to 4:30, except holidays.

The Auditor and Treasurer page says the office produces statements and Truth in Taxation notices for about 23,000 parcels, and holds the levy records for each township, city and school district. Special assessments, ditch records and liens also run through it, as does the tax-forfeited land process, where staff will work with an owner who wants to clear a delinquent balance before forfeiture.

The Assessor's Office carries about 24,500 real estate parcels. Appraisers walk each property at least once in five years, and return sooner after construction or a sale.

Housing in Todd County

Long Prairie is the seat and largest city of this central Minnesota farm and lake county. Population stood at 26,060 in 2025, a 3.1 percent gain on April 2020. Owners occupy 83.0% of the 13,427 housing units, a typical owned home is valued at $207,700, and typical gross rent is $908. Builders pulled just 84 permits in 2025. A lot of housing sits empty part of the year: of 12,770 units in the 2020 count, 22.5 percent were vacant. If you are selling a lake cabin or other seasonal home, ask the assessor how the parcel is classified.

Due dates

On Todd County real estate, the first half is due May 15, the second half of commercial and residential property is due October 15 and the second half of agricultural land is due November 15. Personal property is due in full on May 15.

Todd County payment dates by property type
Property typeFirst paymentSecond payment
Commercial and residential real estateMay 15October 15
Agricultural real estateMay 15November 15
Personal propertyMay 15, in fullNone
Mobile homesAugust 31November 15

When a deadline lands on a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next working day. That is why farmland's second half falls on Monday, November 16 this year: November 15 is a Sunday. For mailed checks, the postmark is what counts, and it must be dated no later than the deadline. Minnesota Statutes 279.01 sets the late charge: 2 percent on homestead tax and 4 percent on nonhomestead tax, growing each month after.

Owners of a class 2a farm should note that agricultural homestead and nonhomestead land may pay its second half by November 15 with no penalty.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Todd County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay Todd County property tax

You can pay online, by phone, in person, by mail or in the payment drop box. The box is at the street-level tunnel entrance of the Historic Courthouse at 215 1st Avenue South.

  • Phone: dial 1-844-368-2607 to reach the automated Point N Pay system.
  • Online: the same vendor takes Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Discover.
  • Fees: the vendor, not the county, keeps a convenience charge. Most cards cost 2.5 percent with a $1.50 minimum, Visa debit is a flat $3.95, and an e-check is $1.50 up to $10,000 and $10.00 above that.
  • Mail: send a check to the Auditor/Treasurer's Office and rely on the postmark as proof.

For parcel details on the current tax year and the current assessment year, use the property information search portal. Call the office numbers above if the portal figures look wrong. Print or save the page you rely on, so you can show a buyer where the figure came from.

How the Todd County Assessor sets a value

Actual sale prices are set against assessed values, and the Assessor then tests whether each district meets state standards. Values are set as of January 2, and a notice goes to each owner in spring with the value, the classification and the steps to appeal.

Most records in the office are public, with exceptions for data covered by the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act. If you are unsure whether something you need is public, ask the office when you call. Forms and applications are online. If one is missing, call 320-732-4431. A seller who disagrees with a notice should call that number before the spring meetings are set.

Appealing a Todd County property value

The sequence is a call to the Assessor, a visit to the local board, and then the county board. Each spring's valuation notice shows the January 2 value and explains how to appeal. Ask the county when this year's board of appeal and equalization will meet.

Minnesota Statutes 274.13 lets the county board cut a value above market, raise one below it and change a class. An exemption is outside its power. If you receive notice of a proposed increase and skip the meeting, you lose the option of taking that value to the state revenue commissioner. Hold on to your evidence, whether an appraisal or comparable sales, since it may serve again next spring. Phone the Assessor at 320-732-4431 well before the meeting, because that call is the cheapest way to learn whether a mistake in the record explains the number on your notice.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Todd County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Questions to settle before you list

  • Which half is still open? Ask the Auditor-Treasurer at 320-732-4469 for the balance on the parcel and whether any special assessment is attached.
  • How is the parcel classified? The Assessor at 320-732-4431 can tell you, and the answer matters most for seasonal or lake property.
  • Is there a ditch or drainage lien? The Auditor-Treasurer keeps those records for the county.
  • Who gets next year's statement? Give the office the buyer's mailing address after the sale.

Write the answers down before you meet a buyer or a title company, along with the parcel number from your statement. A closing moves more smoothly when the tax figures are already settled and nobody is waiting on a phone call to the courthouse.

What a Todd County seller does about the tax bill at closing

Get a statement of the current balance from the Auditor-Treasurer, then decide with the closing agent how to divide the year. A seller usually pays for the days of ownership. Since May 15 and October 15 are the two halves, find out which is still open on your closing date.

Look at special assessments too. The Auditor-Treasurer keeps those that the cities, townships and drainage systems certify, so a ditch lien or a street assessment may remain on the parcel after the sale. If the taxes are escrowed, ask the lender for its payoff letter, and give the Auditor-Treasurer the buyer's mailing address so the next statement arrives at the right place.

In a cash sale the steps are the same minus the lender. The title company gets the balance from the Auditor-Treasurer, pays it out of your proceeds and prorates the year under the contract.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Todd County Assessor's phone number?

320-732-4431. The Auditor-Treasurer, who handles statements and payments, is at 320-732-4469.

When is the Todd County farmland second-half tax due?

November 15 normally. This year it is a Sunday, so the payment is due Monday, November 16.

Can I mail a Todd County tax payment on the due date?

Yes, as long as the postmark carries that date or an earlier one. The county treats the postmark as proof of timely mailing.

What does Todd County charge to pay by credit card?

Most cards carry 2.5 percent with a $1.50 minimum, and Visa debit is a flat $3.95. The vendor collects these fees, not the county.

How many parcels does the Todd County Auditor-Treasurer bill?

About 23,000 parcels. The Assessor's Office keeps records on roughly 24,500 real estate parcels.

Which offices handle property tax

Two desks in the Government Services Building in Mantorville take most questions. Land Records (the assessor) covers value and classification. Finance covers the bill and payments. Both are at 721 Main Street North, Mantorville, MN 55955, with weekday hours from eight in the morning to four-thirty.

  • Assessor (Land Records): 507-635-6245, Dept. 102. Call about estimated market value, classification, homestead and appeal steps.
  • Finance: 507-635-6240, Dept. 45. Call about amounts due, duplicate statements, penalties and past-due balances.

The county runs its parcel and payment lookup through an online tax portal, so you can search by parcel number or street address before calling. Lost statements can be printed there for years back to 2013, and Finance will mail a duplicate if you ask by phone.

Dodge County housing for sellers

Dodge County is in southeastern Minnesota, part of the Rochester metropolitan area. Kasson is the largest city and Mantorville holds the courthouse. Other cities include Blooming Prairie (shared with Steele County), Claremont, Dodge Center, Hayfield and West Concord.

About 21,376 people live here. The county has 8,773 housing units, and owners occupy 86.6 percent of occupied homes. The median owner-occupied value is $287,700 and median household income is near $95,739.

With owners in nearly nine of ten homes, a listing that arrives with an unpaid tax balance or an open classification question is easy for a buyer to spot. Sort out both first.

Due dates and penalties

Residential real estate tax comes in two halves, due May 15 and October 15. Farm land has until November 15 for the second half. Minn. Stat. 279.01 sets those dates and the penalties, so the county cannot waive them by itself.

Mailed checks count on the postmark date, so the county advises handing the envelope across the post office counter to get it hand stamped. A homestead payment that misses its date picks up 2 percent, and non-homestead picks up 4 percent. The penalty jumps again at the start of the next month and then grows by 1 percent monthly through December, stopping at 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for non-homestead property. The treasurer can also abate a first late penalty if the payment was mailed and postmarked within one business day of the deadline.

Dodge County property tax calendar
DateWhat happens
January 2Values are fixed; prior-year balances turn delinquent
March 31Finance finishes mailing real estate statements

December 1 and 15Live in the home by December 1, file for homestead by December 15

Paying a Dodge County bill

Payment can go by mail, at the Administration window, in a drop box, or online. Write checks and money orders to Dodge County and enclose your statement stub. Mail goes to Dodge County Finance, 721 Main Street North, Dept. 45, Mantorville, MN 55955.

  • In person: the Administration window on the main floor accepts cash, money order, cashier's check or personal check.
  • Drop box: to the left of the west-facing main entrance. Write a note on the envelope if you want a receipt.
  • Online: card payments carry a 2.75 percent fee, and an e-check costs $3.99 per transaction. Posting takes one to two business days.

Finance sends no reminders, and only one statement per parcel goes out each year. If yours has not shown up by April 10, call for a duplicate. A missing statement does not remove the penalty.

How to contest a valuation

The day your spring Notice of Valuation and Classification shows up, get an appraiser at the assessor's on the phone. The assessor can change a value only until the local board convenes. After that, relief comes only from a board or the Tax Court.

  1. Local Board of Appeal and Equalization or open book meeting. Your city or township holds one in April or May, with the date printed on the notice. Its reductions cannot lower the assessor's total for the district by more than one percent (Minn. Stat. 274.01).
  2. County Board of Appeal and Equalization. It meets in June, and only owners who appealed at the first level can be heard.
  3. Minnesota Tax Court. The petition is due April 30 of the year the tax is payable (Minn. Stat. 278.01). The Small Claims Division is final, while the Regular Division can be appealed further.

Feeling that the bill is high does not justify a value change. Bring a recent appraisal, comparable sales or errors in the property record instead. Questions about tax levels belong at the December Truth in Taxation meetings.

Homestead status

A homestead class means a lower rate for the owner's own home than for comparable non-homestead property. To get it, present proof of ownership, complete an application and supply the Social Security numbers of all owners. You must be a Minnesota resident and be listed as an owner on county tax records.

Timing matters for a buyer. A buyer who moves in by December 1 and files by December 15 sees homestead rates in the following year's tax. A seller who rented the house before listing may have changed the class, which is why Finance sends "why did my classification change" calls back to Land Records at 507-635-6245. Relatives of an owner can qualify, as can certain trusts and life estates when the deed shows the interest.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Dodge County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Clearing the tax at a sale

At transfer, the auditor first checks whether delinquent tax is owed. Minn. Stat. 272.12 sends the deed to the county auditor first. The auditor searches for delinquent taxes and certifies the land clear, and only then can the recorder take the deed.

For this reason the closing agent wants a payoff number ahead of the signing. If a buyer takes over after statements have been mailed, Dodge County sends a courtesy letter showing that year's tax rather than a full statement, even when a lender escrows the payment. A seller on a contract for deed stays responsible for confirming taxes were paid, although only the new contract holder receives the bill. Ask the title or closing agent how the current year is divided between buyer and seller, since that depends on the purchase agreement.

Back taxes

Call Finance at 507-635-6240 for the exact amount, which includes penalty and interest, or look the parcel up in the portal, where delinquent figures are kept current. Unpaid prior-year tax becomes delinquent on January 2.

Paying before you list usually simplifies the closing. If the amount is more than you can cover, get the exact figure from Finance before the next January 2 so you know what the delinquency date will add.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I send a Dodge County property tax payment?

Mail it to Dodge County Finance, 721 Main Street North, Dept. 45, Mantorville, MN 55955, with the stub from your statement. The postmark must show May 15 or October 15 or earlier, so the county suggests a post office hand stamp.

Is there a fee to pay Dodge County taxes online?

Yes. Card payments carry a 2.75 percent fee and an e-check costs $3.99 per transaction, with several parcels allowed in one e-check. Allow one to two business days to post.

By when must a Dodge County owner file an appeal?

The local board or open book meeting comes first, in April or May, with the date on your valuation notice. A Minnesota Tax Court petition must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

I bought a Dodge County house after statements were mailed. Do I still owe the tax?

Yes. You will receive a courtesy letter instead of a statement, and the tax is still yours to pay by the due dates. Call Finance at 507-635-6240 with your parcel number or address for a copy.

Which office changes my homestead status in Dodge County?

The assessor's office in Land Records, at 507-635-6245. File in person, by phone or by email, or download the form from the county website, and apply by December 15 after owning and living in the home by December 1.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Hubbard County at a glance

Hubbard County sits in northwestern Minnesota, and Park Rapids is the seat. Lakes and woods dominate, and the cities are Akeley, Laporte, Nevis and Park Rapids. Population was 22,369 in the July 2025 estimate, up 4.8% from 2020. There are 14,900 housing units but only 8,964 households, and the 2020 census counted 39.6% of units as vacant, which tells you a big share of homes here are cabins or second homes. Owner occupancy is 83.1% and the median home value is $282,600.

Because so many properties are seasonal, classification is the first thing to check before listing. A cabin or lake home used part of the year is taxed differently from a primary residence.

Which office handles property tax

Two departments share the job. The Auditor/Treasurer runs tax administration, collects delinquent taxes, publishes the delinquent tax list, and handles forfeitures, repurchases and confessions of judgment. The auditor also holds a seat on the county board of equalization.

The assessor works inside Property Records at the Government Center, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470, phone 218-732-3552. That office covers valuation and classification, homestead, tax reduction programs and the recording of real estate documents, so one trip can take care of a value question and a deed together.

Due dates and penalties

Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01, a parcel with more than $100 in tax pays in two halves, one before May 16 and one before October 16. At $100 or less, the whole amount is due with the first half. Mail counts as on time if postmarked by the deadline, and the treasurer has to waive the penalty one time if the postmark is a single business day late.

Late penalties on an unpaid half
StageHomesteadNonhomestead
Day after the due date2%4%
First day of the next monthAnother 2%Another 4%
Each month after, through December1% more1% more
Ceiling8%12%

Agricultural homestead and qualifying farm land may pay the second half through November 15 with no penalty. Seasonal residential recreational property that is not used commercially, which the statute calls class 4c, is charged the lower homestead penalty rates.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hubbard County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead for buyers and sellers

The county has posted a homestead notice for the 2026 assessment. Someone who bought or moved into a home in the past year must apply by December 31, 2026 for the benefit to reach taxes payable in 2027, and the applicant needs to have owned and lived in the home by that date. A relative living there also qualifies. For residential and agricultural property, that means the owner's or spouse's child, grandchild, sibling or parent, plus the owner's uncle, aunt, nephew or niece.

  • File online, in person or by mail. Once granted, the application does not need repeating unless the assessor asks.
  • Each occupant, owner and spouse signs and supplies a Social Security number, so the state can confirm no other Minnesota homestead is claimed.
  • The driver's license must show the home address, because Minnesota requires an address change within 30 days.
  • A relative homestead does not qualify for the property tax refund. A property that was ever classified seasonal residential recreational under the current owner cannot take a relative homestead.

If you move out or stop qualifying, tell the assessor within 30 days. Miss that and the parcel can be recalculated as nonhomestead, with a penalty equal to 100 percent of the homestead benefit.

How to dispute your valuation

Call the assessor at 218-732-3552 first. After that, Minnesota Statutes 274.01 provides two stages. The local board of appeal and equalization, which is the town board or city council unless it has handed the job to the county, meets between April 1 and May 31 after at least ten days of published notice. It has 20 days from convening to finish, and its reductions cannot lower the assessor's total by more than one percent.

Skip the local board after being notified and you generally lose the right to appear at the county board, so the spring meeting is worth attending. A late disagreement goes to the county board of equalization, where the auditor serves. The last stop is Tax Court, and a district court petition for a given tax year is due April 30 of that year under Statutes 278.01.

Dates coming up

  • November 15: last day to pay the second half on qualifying agricultural property without penalty.
  • December: unpaid halves pick up another 1 percent each month until they reach the cap for the property type.
  • December 31, 2026: final day to apply for homestead on a home you owned and lived in during the year.
  • April 30, 2027: court filing date for a petition about taxes payable in 2027, which follows the March valuation notice.

If you close before December 31, mention the homestead deadline to the buyer. The buyer's own application is what carries the benefit into 2027 taxes, and the assessor at 218-732-3552 can mail or email the form.

Before you list a Hubbard County property

Start with the classification. Ask the assessor at 218-732-3552 whether the parcel is taxed as homestead, seasonal recreational or something else, because that one answer sets the penalty rates and the homestead rules a buyer will face. Next, find out which halves are paid. The Auditor/Treasurer can tell you whether anything is open from earlier years and whether the parcel appears on the published delinquent tax list.

Then plan the handoff. Give the buyer the date of the homestead deadline if your closing falls before it, and keep a copy of your latest statement for the title company. Doing these three things before a showing keeps the paperwork from slowing the sale later.

What a seller settles at closing

Delinquent tax gets paid before recording. Hubbard's recorder asks for this, and Minnesota Statutes 272.12 stops the auditor from transferring a parcel that still has delinquent tax on it. Current-year tax is not required at recording unless the parcel is being split, and it is usually collected through the closing settlement. Tax payments are not part of electronic recording, so your title company arranges the payoff separately.

The recorder takes abstract and Torrens documents through four trusted submitters: ePN, Indecomm Global Services, Corporation Service Company and Simplifile. State deed tax and mortgage registration tax are collected together with the recording fee. A deed uses an eCRV and, when needed, an electronic well disclosure certificate. For a current-year payoff figure, ask the Hubbard County Treasurer's Office, and ask the assessor how your lake home is classified, since that decides the penalty rates and homestead rules.

If the house is inherited, empty or behind on taxes, bring the parcel number and latest statement to the Auditor/Treasurer and ask what is owed through your expected closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Hubbard County property tax?

At the Auditor/Treasurer in the Government Center in Park Rapids, or online through the Pay Your Taxes Online link on the county's I want to Pay page. Mailed payments need a postmark by the due date.

Does a Hubbard County cabin qualify for homestead?

Only if you own it and live there as your primary home, or a qualifying relative does. Seasonal residential recreational property is its own class, and a relative homestead is barred on any property that has carried that class under the current owner.

When must I apply for Hubbard County homestead?

By December 31, 2026 for the current assessment, which affects taxes payable in 2027. You must own and occupy the property by then, and you can apply online, in person or by mail.

Are Hubbard County property taxes paid at closing?

Often, yes, through the settlement statement, though current-year tax is not required at recording unless the parcel is split. Delinquent tax must be paid before the deed is recorded.

What is the Hubbard County assessor's phone number?

218-732-3552, at Property Records, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470. The same office handles valuation, classification, homestead and recording.

What the Lyon County Assessor does

Every parcel gets a market value and a class from the Assessor's Office, 607 West Main Street, Marshall, MN 56258, effective January 2. Under state rules each property must be looked at in person at least once every five years, which the county organizes as a quintile review. Notices of value reach owners in spring, and boards of equalization at the local, county and state level meet yearly for anyone contesting value or class.

The same office runs the Green Acres, blind or disabled homestead and local option disaster abatement programs, and takes homestead applications.

What the Auditor/Treasurer handles

Besides running county finances and elections, the Auditor/Treasurer administers property tax. That covers calculating each bill, collecting current and delinquent real estate tax, managing escrow, distributing receipts to the taxing entities, handling forfeited land proceedings and special assessments, ditches included.

By statute this officer also sits on the County Board of Equalization. The county's online tools let you find and pay your property tax and search property records, valuation, classification and sales information. If your parcel has ditch assessments, ask this office to itemize them.

Lyon County housing in brief

The county seat is Marshall, and the county forms the Marshall Micropolitan Statistical Area. Other cities are Balaton, Cottonwood, Florence, Garvin, Ghent, Lynd, Minneota, Russell, Taunton and Tracy. The July 2025 population estimate is 25,684, just 0.6% above 2020.

The county has 11,437 housing units, with only 23 building permits issued in 2025. Owners live in 72.5% of homes, and the 2020 census counted 33.6% of occupied units as rented, so renters make up a good share of households. The median owner-occupied home is worth $200,700 and median gross rent is $781. The median home value is $200,700, so compare your assessed value with your asking price early.

Due dates and penalty rules

The state calendar applies in Lyon County: one half before May 16, one before October 16, for any bill above $100. At $100 or less, you pay once, by the spring date.

Payment or situationRule
First halfBefore May 16

The treasurer may accept a payment larger or smaller than the exact installment. A short payment goes first to the oldest installment still owed, and to accrued penalty before tax. A homestead owner in the National Guard or a reserve component on federal active service gets a four-month grace period with no penalty, and must send a copy of orders or form DD214 with the payment.

Ditches and special assessments

Lyon County parcels can carry charges that never show up in a value notice. The Auditor/Treasurer handles special assessments, ditches among them, and can list each one for a given parcel. Rural sellers in particular should ask for that itemized list before pricing the house, since a buyer's lender or attorney will ask for the same figures.

Special assessments travel with the parcel. If a balance is still open when you sell, the payoff at closing has to cover it, or the purchase contract has to say plainly who takes it on. Getting the number in writing from the county avoids an argument at the table. Ask the Auditor/Treasurer whether any ditch assessment is still being certified, and add the answer to your listing file so a buyer's questions are met with facts rather than guesses.

Homestead applications

Fill out the homestead application online and print it, or print a blank form and complete it by hand. Mail it to the Lyon County Assessor's Office, 607 West Main Street, Marshall, MN 56258, or leave it in the drop box at the rear entrance of the Lyon County Government Center.

One local exception: a property inside the City of Marshall files by calling 507-537-6771. Homestead is the program the county is asked about most, and the Assessor has a plain-language FAQ on what it is and why it matters. Classification counts most when a payment is late, because the penalty on a nonhomestead parcel starts at 4% instead of 2%.

The state Homestead Credit Refund is a separate benefit from the Department of Revenue. It is due August 15 and can be filed for up to one year after that date.

How to appeal a Lyon County valuation

Start by reading the spring notice and phoning the assessor with your evidence. Anything left unsettled goes to the local, county or state board of equalization. The Assessor's FAQ page walks through each step, including what evidence to bring.

Court is governed by Minnesota Statutes section 278.01. A district court petition has to be served on the county auditor and filed with the court administrator by April 30 of the payable year. Tax Court appeals open once the notice arrives and must be started before May 1. Notice of a change in value or class that comes after February 28 gives you 60 days from the date it was mailed.

A simple timeline for sellers

Early in the year, check your January 2 value against the notice that arrives in the spring, and call the assessor if the number looks wrong. By May, make sure the first half is paid, because a nonhomestead parcel starts picking up a 4% penalty the next day. Through the summer, gather your record card and tax statements while you prepare to list. By October, pay the second half or know exactly what is open.

When you have an accepted offer, give your closing agent the parcel number and ask the Auditor/Treasurer for a payoff dated to the closing day. Agricultural owners should remember their second half can run to November 15 without penalty, which can change how a closing in late fall is handled.

Before you close on a Lyon County sale

Ask the Auditor/Treasurer for the amount owed on your parcel, including penalty and any ditch or other special assessment, and compare it with your closing date. Ask the Assessor whether the homestead classification still matches how the house is used.

The Assessor's online property search shows the property record card, valuation, classification and characteristics for a parcel, and a separate tax information page shows statements and sales. Print the record card before you list, so the numbers you quote match the county's.

If the house is inherited, vacant or behind on taxes, add one step: ask for the full balance, not just the current half. Anything unpaid from earlier years has to be cleared before the sale can finish, whether the buyer uses a mortgage or pays cash.

Where do I mail a Lyon County homestead application?

Send it to the Lyon County Assessor's Office, 607 West Main Street, Marshall, MN 56258. There is also a drop box at the rear entrance of the Lyon County Government Center.

Who do I call to file homestead for a house inside Marshall?

Call 507-537-6771. Properties within the City of Marshall file through that number.

How often does the Lyon County assessor inspect a property?

At least once every five years under Minnesota law. The county uses a quintile review that includes an in-person visit to the property.

What is the court deadline to challenge a Lyon County tax?

April 30 of the year the tax is payable for a district court petition. A Tax Court appeal must begin before May 1, under Minnesota Statutes section 278.01.

What is the largest late penalty on a Lyon County rental?

12% of the unpaid tax, the cap for nonhomestead property under Minnesota Statutes section 279.01. A homestead is capped at 8%.

Morrison County housing in brief

Morrison County is a mostly rural, river-and-lake county in central Minnesota, and Little Falls is both the seat and the biggest town. The Mississippi River runs south through the western part, and Camp Ripley Military Reservation fills a big piece of the north-central area. The county covers about 1,125 square miles of land.

The July 2025 population estimate is 34,620, with 16,659 housing units. Owners live in 80.6 percent of occupied homes. For 2020 to 2024 the middle owner-occupied home value was $248,500, middle gross rent was $788 a month, and the median household earned $69,446. The county issued 156 building permits in 2025. That middle value covers the whole county, so your own house may sit far from it.

Ask the Assessor's Office what classification your parcel carries before you list. Classification and estimated market value are the two things an owner may contest.

Offices in Little Falls

All three offices share the Government Center at 213 1st Avenue SE, Little Falls, MN 56345. The county switchboard is 320-632-2941, with a toll-free line at 1-866-401-1111, and front-line county offices post weekday hours from 8 to 4:30.

  • Auditor/Treasurer: sends the tax bills, collects the money and holds the payment counter.
  • Assessor's Office (Land Services): sets estimated market value and classification, and answers value questions at 320-632-0170.

Online, the county directs people to Beacon for maps and tax statements, and to Landshark for recorded documents.

Payment deadlines

Two installments make up the real property bill, due May 15 and October 15, with extra dates for resorts, manufactured homes and farmland. Personal property and severed mineral interest taxes fall due alongside the real property installments. A deadline that lands on a weekend or legal holiday shifts to the next day the office is open.

Morrison County tax due dates
DateWhat is due
May 15Real property, first installment, or the entire bill if it totals $100 or under
May 31Resort property, first half
August 31Manufactured homes, first installment, or the entire bill if it totals $50 or under
October 15Non-agricultural real property, second half
November 15Agricultural real property and manufactured homes, second half

Minn. Stat. 279.01 uses the same May and October split for bills above $100, and lets agricultural homestead and a few related classes pay the second half through November 15 without penalty.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Morrison County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay

Six channels are open:

  • Counter: cash or a check made out to Morrison County Auditor/Treasurer, during office hours.
  • Drop box: at Broadway (Highway 27) and 2nd Street SE, emptied every day.
  • Postal mail: addressed to the Auditor/Treasurer at the Government Center. The postmark is treated as proof of timely mailing.
  • Direct Debit: an enrollment form the county needs 30 days ahead of a due date.
  • Card or eCheck online: American Express, Discover, MasterCard and Visa.
  • Phone: 888-272-9829, then jurisdiction code 3314. Press 1 for personal property, 2 for real estate or 3 for mobile homes.

Fees on electronic payments are 2.59 percent for credit cards, 2.59 percent for debit cards with a $1.10 floor, and $2.15 for an eCheck.

What a late payment costs

Miss an installment deadline and the bill grows by 2 percent for a homestead or 4 percent for any other property. Section 279.01 charges the same again if the balance is still open when the next month starts, then adds 1 percent each month until December. A homestead tops out at 8 percent, everything else at 12 percent.

Mailed payments get one break. If the Postal Service postmarked the envelope no more than a business day after the deadline, the treasurer must forgive the penalty, once per owner. If the postmark is missing or smudged, a signed affidavit from the owner can establish the mailing date. The county board can also let the treasurer waive a penalty that would be unjust and unreasonable, so ask the Auditor/Treasurer about that policy.

What to do if your valuation looks too high

Do your homework before any hearing. What you can appeal is the current estimated market value or the classification, both of which drive next year's taxes, and recent comparable sales are the best thing to bring.

  1. Collect comparable recent sales.
  2. Call the Assessor's Office, 320-632-0170, and walk a county appraiser through your numbers.
  3. If that fails, request a slot with your local appeal board, which meets in April.
  4. Still unhappy? Book the special appeal board, which sits in June. It will only hear you after the local board has.
  5. The final route is Minnesota Tax Court.

Hearing dates are printed on the valuation notice and run in local papers. A dispute over last year's value cannot go to the assessor. It goes to Tax Court only, and must be filed there by the end of April of the year the bill comes due.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Morrison County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Does a sale change the tax picture?

Yes, twice over: the deed has to pass a tax check, and homestead status resets. Minn. Stat. 272.12 routes every deed past the auditor before recording, and the auditor looks for unpaid delinquent tax and marks the deed. Without that mark the recorder cannot accept it.

A price above $3,000 also calls for a certificate of value, which section 272.115 has the buyer or seller hand to the auditor. The assessor then takes homestead status off the parcel for the following assessment year, unless the new owner applies and qualifies. With no application on file by December 31, the parcel is treated as nonhomestead that year.

Owing back tax, or holding an inherited or as-is property, is a reason to phone the Auditor/Treasurer for a payoff figure with penalties included. Ask whoever runs your closing how this year's bill will be split.

Steps before you list

Find your latest statement and note the parcel number. Then ask the Auditor/Treasurer whether both installments are paid and whether any earlier year is open. Ask the Assessor for the parcel's class and its estimated market value, and compare those with your asking price. If your closing falls near a due date, use the card, eCheck, phone or counter options rather than mail, so the payment posts before the deadline.

At the title company, expect questions about the certificate of value and about who covers each part of the current year. A buyer who plans to live in the house should file a homestead application, because without one the parcel is treated as nonhomestead for the next assessment year, and the penalty rate and the tax rate both change.

Frequently asked questions

Which number reaches the Morrison County assessor?

The assessor's line is 320-632-0170. For payments and balances, use the Government Center switchboard at 320-632-2941 and ask for the Auditor/Treasurer.

When does the last Morrison County installment fall due?

October 15 closes out non-agricultural real property. Farmland and manufactured homes run to November 15, and a date that falls on a weekend moves to the next business day.

Can I use a credit card on my Morrison County tax bill?

Yes. Use the county's online payment link or call 888-272-9829 and enter jurisdiction code 3314. Expect a 2.59 percent convenience charge on a credit card.

What is the order of Morrison County appeal steps?

The assessor first, then the April local board, then the June special board, and finally Minnesota Tax Court. The special board hears only people who already went to the local board.

Can I sell a Morrison County house that owes back taxes?

Yes, once the delinquent tax is paid. A deed cannot be recorded without the auditor's mark showing no delinquent tax, so ask the Auditor/Treasurer for a payoff figure with penalties included.

Where to take property tax questions

Both property tax offices sit in the courthouse at 130 E. Minnesota Avenue in Glenwood. The Assessor, at 320-634-7715, sets the estimated market value and the class of each parcel. The Auditor/Treasurer, at 320-634-7706, prepares and mails the statements, takes payments and manages delinquent accounts. Each year the office mails more than 13,500 real estate and mobile home statements and collects over $14,000,000.

The office keeps weekday hours from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The same counter handles a change of taxpayer name or address, an ACH form for twice-a-year automatic withdrawal, and the sale of tax-forfeited land.

Sellers usually need both offices, so write down both numbers before you list. The Assessor explains a value or a homestead question, and the Auditor/Treasurer supplies the balance that must be cleared before a deed can move.

Selling a house in Pope County

Pope County is farm and lake country in west central Minnesota, and Glenwood is the county seat and largest city. Population is 11,420, a 1.0% gain since 2020. There are 6,549 housing units, and 83.5% are occupied by owners. Median value of an owner-occupied home is $255,100, and median household income is $76,220.

Only 33 building permits were issued in 2025, and 27.5% of residents are 65 or older. With few new homes being built, resale sellers here are often handling a parent's house or a lake property with an older owner.

The 2027 levy

On September 15, 2026 the County Board set a preliminary 2027 levy of $11,809,106, which is 3.4% above the 2026 levy of $11,420,799. State law lets the county hold or lower that figure at final adoption but not raise it.

The Truth-in-Taxation hearing is scheduled for Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. at the courthouse. Each parcel gets a single proposed-tax notice from the Auditor/Treasurer, but the county decides only the county line. City, township, school and special district proposals have their own hearings, and those dates are printed on the notice.

How to appeal your valuation

Spring is the moment to act, when the valuation notice arrives with the tax statement. By the time proposed taxes come out in the fall it is too late. The usual route has these stops:

  • Call the Assessor at 320-634-7715 and discuss the value or class informally. Informal appeals run until the special County Board meeting in early June.
  • Go to your local board of appeal and equalization. Local meetings are by appointment through the Assessor, and some areas, such as Glenwood, hold an open book session at the Assessor's Office in April.
  • Appear before the County Board of Appeal and Equalization, which meets in the courthouse board room in June. Speakers need an appointment made a few days ahead through the Assessor.

State law puts the burden of proof on the owner. Your evidence has to be strong enough to show the Assessor's number is wrong, and only relevant testimony given at the board counts. Bring a recent appraisal, photos of defects, or sales of similar homes nearby, and keep your remarks on the value and class of your own parcel rather than on the size of the tax bill.

Due dates and late penalties

Real estate tax is paid in halves, with the first due May 15 and the second due October 15. The second half on class 2a agricultural land is not due until November 15. Pope County does not mail second-half statements, so the stub from the spring mailing is what you send back in the fall. Taxes of $100 or less must be paid in full with the first half.

The statement lists the penalty ladder for homestead and cabin property:

Pope County late penalties on homestead and cabin property
Paid afterFirst half unpaidSecond half unpaid
May 162%not yet due
June 14%not yet due
July 15%not yet due
August 16%not yet due
September 17%not yet due
October 18%not yet due
October 168%2%
November 18%4%
December 18%5%

Nonhomestead land carries double the early rates, starting at 4% after May 15. The office cannot accept post-dated checks, a postmark from the Postal Service proves timely mailing, and a private meter postmark does not.

Other charges on the statement

Bills here include a solid waste fee. For the 2026 payable year it was $139 on any property with a building value of $5,000 or more, collected for the Pope/Douglas Solid Waste Management system at 320-763-9340. It is a charge listed apart from the value-based tax.

The homestead exclusion works as a reduction of taxable value. On the 2026 statement it peaks at $38,000 for a home valued at $95,000, shrinks by nine percent of the value above that, and disappears at $517,200. Special assessments for streets, sidewalks and sewers appear in their own section, and they are based on benefit to the property, not market value.

Many bills are paid through a lender's escrow account. The county mails the owner a copy anyway and sends the lender its own listing.

Tax relief and selling the house

Two state refunds exist for homesteads owned and occupied on January 2. The regular refund applies when taxes exceed income-based thresholds and household income is under $142,490. The special refund applies when net tax on the homestead rose more than 12% and the increase was at least $100. Both use Form M1PR, due August 15. A senior deferral is also offered for owners 65 or older with household income of $96,000 or less who have lived in the home five years; the filing date is November 1 of the year before the tax is payable.

Sellers should ask the Auditor/Treasurer for a payoff before listing. If the property is a mobile home, the ownership-change form requires the entire parcel's taxes to be paid, and both the Auditor/Treasurer and the Assessor must sign before the Department of Motor Vehicles can transfer the title.

Bring the parcel number and your expected closing date when you ask, and get the figure in writing. A cash sale has no lender payoff letter to wait on, so the county's balance is the main item to clear.

Frequently asked questions

What number do I call to dispute a Pope County property value?

The Assessor's Office at 320-634-7715. Call before the early June special board meeting for an informal review, and make an appointment if you plan to speak at the County Board of Appeal and Equalization.

Does Pope County mail a bill for the second half?

No. Second-half statements are not mailed. Use the second-half stub from the statement you received in the spring, and mail it or bring it in by October 15.

What is the Pope County solid waste fee?

It is a charge on properties with a building value of $5,000 or more that supports the Pope/Douglas Solid Waste Management system. It was $139 for the 2026 taxes payable year. Call 320-763-9340 with questions about the fee.

When is the Pope County Truth-in-Taxation hearing?

Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. at the courthouse in Glenwood. Other taxing bodies hold separate hearings listed on your proposed notice.

Can I pay Pope County property tax automatically?

Yes, through the ACH Real Estate Tax Payment Form on the Auditor/Treasurer's page. It deducts payments from a checking or savings account twice a year. Return the completed form to the office.

Where to take a Wabasha County tax bill

The Auditor/Treasurer's counter sits at 625 Jefferson Avenue in the city of Wabasha, with weekday hours from eight in the morning to four in the afternoon. The Assessor shares that address and answers questions about value and class at 651-565-3669. To get a copy of a statement, ring 651-565-2648, or use the Beacon lookup linked from the county's statement page with a parcel number or street address.

The payment page offers several routes:

  • The web at www.co.wabasha.mn.us/paytax, or the phone line 1-866-539-2020 (bureau code 8190128) between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday to Friday; keep the parcel number and amount handy, and expect a convenience fee from the card processor
  • Direct Payment Plan (ACH) drafts from a checking or savings account, with forms at the office or through 651-565-4410
  • The brown mailbox-style drop box standing in front of the courthouse
  • A mailed check with the stub, bearing a postmark that is not later than the due date
  • A visit to the counter with cash, check, money order, e-check or a card

If you move, even for a short stay, give the county the new address. The Post Office returns undeliverable statements and notices to the courthouse rather than forwarding them.

Housing in Wabasha County

Wabasha County lines the Mississippi River in southeastern Minnesota and takes in part of Lake Pepin. The city of Wabasha is the seat, and Lake City is the biggest city. Population was 21,537 in July 2025, up 0.8% from the 2020 base. There are 10,439 housing units, owners live in 83.3% of them, and the median home value is $264,400. Median gross rent is $830. Builders took out only 51 permits in 2025.

Few new houses arrive and the population skews older, so sellers here often hold an inherited farmhouse, a retiree's place or a home left empty after a move. Each of those still needs a clean tax record before the deed goes to the recorder. If the owner has died or moved away, find out where statements have been going, because an unopened bill can mean unpaid tax and penalty on a parcel nobody is watching.

Due dates

Real estate is payable in two parts. A due date that lands on a weekend moves to the Monday after it. The October 15 date for ordinary real estate has already passed this year.

Wabasha County payment calendar
Type of propertyFirst paymentSecond payment
Real estate, most classesMay 15October 15
Classified agriculturalMay 15November 15
Mobile (manufactured) homesAugust 31November 15
Prior-year tax left unpaidTurns delinquent January 2

Statements are mailed at the end of March, and mobile home statements follow, with July 15 as the assessor's mailing deadline for those. Someone who buys after the mailing gets no statement. The office sends a courtesy letter with the year's tax, and it does so even when a lender is paying out of escrow.

What paying late costs

Minnesota Statutes 279.01 adds 2% to a missed homestead installment and 4% to a non-homestead one. A matching amount lands on the first of the following month, then 1% per month after that, topping out at 8% for homestead and 12% for non-homestead. The reverse side of the county statement prints its own table.

The county does not waive these penalties, since the rates come from the Legislature. About two weeks after a missed date the office mails a courtesy notice with the tax owed and the penalty accrued. The statute carves out one exception: mail postmarked within a single business day of the deadline gets the penalty abated, once per owner. Tax still open on January 2 is delinquent, and that balance follows the parcel into any sale.

How can I dispute a Wabasha County value?

The county values property as of January 2. Market value notices go out in March, April and May, at least ten days ahead of the local board meeting, and those local boards sit from April 1 through May 31. A phone call to the assessor at 651-565-3669 comes first, and it also covers questions on why a home lost its homestead class.

  1. Appear before the board in your city or township, if one exists, with an appraisal or recent comparable sales.
  2. Move up to the county-level board, which meets in the final ten meeting days of June after the second Friday. The valuation notice prints the times.
  3. Or file in Minnesota Tax Court. The petition must be served on the county auditor under section 278.01, and April 30 is the final filing date for current taxes.

Mobile homes taxed as personal property run on a separate clock: September 1 is the Tax Court deadline for a valuation petition. Whatever route you pick, keep paying the tax on schedule while the dispute is open.

How a Wabasha County closing handles the tax bill

Before the recorder accepts a deed, the auditor looks for delinquent tax. Section 272.12 bars recording unless the document carries the note that no delinquent taxes are due. Any back tax must be paid by the time of signing. Ring the Auditor/Treasurer at 651-565-2648 for the balance while the date is still open.

The split of the current year between seller and buyer comes out of the purchase agreement and the closing statement, so confirm it with the title agent or attorney. Heirs clearing out a parent's house should note that statements travel to the address on file, which may be a house nobody is checking mail at anymore.

A cash sale does not skip this step. The auditor's check happens before any deed is recorded, so ask for the balance early and have it cleared at signing.

Other filing dates for Wabasha County homeowners

The assessor's dates and deadlines page names several that have nothing to do with the two payments:

  • February 1: filing an exemption from taxation
  • May 1: Green Acres deferment for the next year's taxes
  • July 1: disability homestead exclusion and the senior deferral
  • August 15: the state Property Tax Refund, form M-1PR
  • October 1: special homestead class for the blind or the permanently and totally disabled
  • December 31: establishing homestead for the current assessment

Proposed-tax notices are mailed by November 24. Local governments then hold budget hearings from November 29 through December 20, and that is the stage at which a resident can speak on next year's levy.

Frequently asked questions

Which Wabasha County tax date is coming up?

Monday, November 16, for second-half agricultural and mobile home tax, since November 15 is a Sunday. Ordinary real estate was due October 15. For a balance, call 651-565-2648.

Do new buyers in Wabasha County get a statement in the mail?

Not if the purchase happens after the March mailing. A courtesy letter with the year's tax arrives instead, whether or not a lender escrows. Confirm the figure with the Auditor/Treasurer.

Does the county ever forgive a late fee?

Rarely. State law fixes the rates, so the county does not waive them. The statutory exception covers a payment mailed with a postmark within one business day of the deadline, once per owner.

Whom should I ask about a jump in my assessed value?

The Assessor, at 651-565-3669, in the courthouse at 625 Jefferson Avenue in Wabasha. Gather an appraisal or comparable sales first, because the office will usually want to inspect the property.

By when must a Tax Court petition be filed in Wabasha County?

April 30 for current taxes on real and personal property. A mobile home assessed as personal property has a September 1 deadline. In both cases the county auditor must be served.

Paying your Winona County tax bill

The Auditor-Treasurer's office is on the main floor of the Winona County Office Building, 202 West Third Street in Winona. It opens from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. Make checks out to the Winona County Auditor-Treasurer. For tax questions, call 507-457-8830. The county's property taxes page covers online payment.

Winona County payment methods and what each one costs
MethodCost to the taxpayerNotes
Credit card online2.4% convenience feeCharged by the card processor, not the county
Debit card online1.5% convenience feeSame processor
Electronic check onlineFlat $1.50Online, through the county's payment link
Check by mail or drop boxNo feeInclude the stub; the drop box is on the Washington Street side
Automatic ACHNo feePulls from your account on the due date; call to enroll

The exterior deposit slot and the counter box inside are closed after each tax due date. Penalty is added the next day, so after a deadline you need to come inside, call, or look up the amount online before you pay.

Replacing a lost statement

Open the county's Beacon page from the pay online link and search by parcel number (the xx.xxx.xxxx digits on your statement) or by address. Scroll to the Tax Statement section, where the last few years appear as PDF links. To change your mailing address, use the county's online form, call 507-457-8830, or write it on the back of a payment stub.

Winona County at a glance

Winona County sits on the Mississippi River in southeastern Minnesota, and the city of Winona is both the county seat and the largest city. Two colleges, Winona State University and Saint Mary's University of Minnesota, give the city a college-town feel. The county had 50,523 residents in July 2025, about 1.7% above the 2020 base. Of 22,003 housing units, only 69.5% are owner-occupied. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $235,400, and median gross rent is $907.

Nearly a third of households rent (31.9% at the 2020 census), so many Winona sellers are landlords. Their tax bills follow the same calendar as an owner-occupant's, but a rental generally lacks homestead status. That changes both the property class and the penalty tier.

When Winona County taxes are due

Dates can shift slightly when they land on a weekend. The Auditor-Treasurer runs three schedules:

  • Real estate: May 15 for the first half and October 15 for the second
  • Agricultural property: May 15 and November 15
  • Mobile homes: August 31 and November 15

If you are behind on a house, call 507-457-8830. Under section 279.01 a penalty starts accruing the day after the due date.

If your lender escrows, the payment stub will say so, and the lender learns the amount by file or printout. Don't forward the statement to the mortgage company. Keep it for your records.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Winona County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the assessor sets your home's value

The Assessor's department, at 202 West Third Street and 507-457-6300, values property with a computerized mass appraisal system built on sales. For a house it weighs square footage, bedrooms and bathrooms, age and condition, basement finish, garage size, fireplaces and the land. State standards allow values between 90 and 105 percent of market, measured across all sales and not any one house.

Market swings usually move a value more than improvements do. Added rooms, a finished basement, a major kitchen or bath remodel, new siding or windows, and central air all raise it. Painting, a new water heater, shingling a roof or repairing porch steps generally don't, though several together might. If you're selling, small repairs before listing are unlikely to change the tax value, and the assessor's number isn't an offer price.

How to challenge your valuation

Phone the assessor after the late March valuation notice arrives. Staff will explain how the figure was reached and may ask to inspect the house. Formal appeal meetings follow in April, and the county board then sits as the Board of Appeal and Equalization in June.

A Tax Court route also exists. Under section 278.01 the petition goes on the county auditor and must be filed with the court administrator by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-457-8830 how the office accepts service of a petition.

  1. Call the assessor first and ask how the value was built.
  2. Gather recent sales of similar houses nearby, plus any repair estimates.
  3. Attend the April local appeal meeting or the June county board session.
  4. If you still disagree, file in Tax Court by April 30.

Taxes at a Winona County closing

In a typical sale, taxes are prorated and the buyer is credited with the seller's share. Confirm the numbers on the closing statement or with your realtor or attorney. Delinquent tax has to be paid at closing, and current tax does not. Under section 272.12 the recorder can't take a deed without the auditor's notation that no delinquent taxes remain.

Mobile homes need an extra step. The sale calls for a county statement saying all delinquent and current taxes are paid in full, which comes from the Auditor-Treasurer. If you hold a stray statement, hand it to the new owners, who need it to pay.

A cash buyer who skips the mortgage still faces the same tax steps. The auditor's notation and the proration work identically, but there's no lender payoff or escrow account to unwind, so the closing can move quicker once the title is clear.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Winona County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead and refund rules

Homestead treatment requires that the owner or a qualifying relative own and live in the home as the principal residence. Ownership and occupancy must be in place by December 1 of the year before taxes are payable, and a new homestead application is due by December 15. The assessor's page offers regular and relative homestead forms, a special classification for the blind or disabled, Green Acres paperwork and a mold damage reduction form.

A Property Tax Refund requires state form M1PR, available at the county office or from the Minnesota Department of Revenue at 651-296-4444 or 800-657-3676.

If you sell mid-year, the new owner will need to file their own homestead application by the December 15 deadline. A buyer who moves in after December 1 won't get homestead for the next payable year unless they meet the ownership and occupancy tests by then, so ask your buyer about timing.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Winona County tax drop box?

On the Washington Street side of the Winona County Office Building at 202 West Third Street, to the right of the entry doors. A second box sits on the counter inside. Both are closed after each due date.

Does Winona County charge a fee to pay by card?

Yes, through its payment vendor: 2.4% for credit cards, 1.5% for debit cards and a flat $1.50 for e-check. The county neither charges nor receives those fees. Checks and ACH carry no fee.

Do I have to pay Winona County taxes at closing?

Only delinquent tax must be paid at closing. Current-year tax is normally prorated, with the buyer credited for the seller's portion, but the closing statement controls. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-457-8830 for any status check.

What paperwork does a Winona County mobile home sale need?

The county's own statement confirming that all delinquent and current taxes are paid in full. Request it from the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-457-8830 before you schedule the closing.

What is the Winona County homestead application deadline?

December 15 for a new homestead, provided you met the ownership and occupancy tests by December 1 of the preceding year. Forms are on the Assessor's page or at the office, 507-457-6300.

Cook County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Cook County?
